audit: Checked once on 2026-11-26 by three AI agents that had not written the sheets, against the saved texts. They covered 70 sheets, which include all 69 published here, and reported 121 findings, 24 of them marked wrong; the corrections were applied. Several false or unsupported claims that a named work contained errors were removed or reworded. The check was partial for long documents (targeted sections and searches, not every page listed as read), figures were not examined, and links, DOIs and bibliographic details were not verified online. The corrections were not audited again, corrected fields were not matched to quotes again, and the cross-study synthesis was not independently audited. No human has checked the sheets. One thesis sheet was left out because the thesis asks for the author's permission before material from it is published (its catalogue record stays in the map).

playbooks.title: Simulation-assisted hazard identification and safeguard studies (HAZOP, LOPA, process safety time)
playbooks.intro: In these works a simulator is mostly used to say what a deviation does, how far it goes and how fast, rather than to replace the team study.

points.text: One route sweeps a deviation over a continuous range in a flowsheet model, not as a single high or low case. This can expose jumps between operating branches in reactive units.

The model's own limits matter for the safety conclusion: the same authors later revisit their earlier simulations and show why model-parameter uncertainty such as reaction enthalpy should be carried through the deviation study.

Dynamic response can change the screening result. Reactor studies simulate controller action and transients because a steady-state view does not show whether control moves a mild deviation into an unstable region.

Boundary specifications and automatically inserted controllers decide what a dynamic model can show. In one air-separation study, holding pressures fixed gave a flow trend the thesis calls opposite to real plant behaviour.

Process safety time from a dynamic simulator depends on stated start and end points and on modelling choices such as the pipe pressure-drop correlation. Report each alarm, trip and relief time separately, and treat influential choices as sensitivity cases.

A reconstruction of a past accident can be checked against recorded quantities; one overfill study used a deliberately simplified equipment surrogate and compared level and temperature with the investigation record and another model.
Several of these sheets record no comparison with plant or test data for the dynamic response itself, so the simulated timing is an unvalidated model output there.
Inherent-safety indices are scored from a flowsheet's streams and inventories. The inventory basis and each sub-score need to be traceable.

playbooks.title: Relief, flare, blowdown, runaway and other dynamic models
playbooks.intro: These studies depend on transient behaviour, so what was fitted and what was predicted needs to be kept apart.

points.text: For an existing plant, one flare-study method first rates the dynamic models against the normal historical operating range, then applies stated rules for each scenario's failures and the credit given to controllers.
The coldest case for piping may not be simultaneous full-plant blowdown: partial blowdowns, liquid low points, connected units and sensor placement all matter when comparing with measurements.

In blowdown validation, pressure agreement is weak evidence when a discharge coefficient or relaxation time was fitted to the same test. Minimum temperature and its timing, and held-out tests, are the stronger checks.
Heat transfer, thermocouple response and behaviour near the CO2 triple point each need checking before a temperature mismatch is blamed on one cause.

Runaway vent sizing by dynamic simulation was checked against small-scale tests, which agreed without an exhaust line and differed with one. By contrast, steady-state feed sensitivities alone do not show a transient runaway.

Start-up, compressor and operator-training models are compared with plant records. Logged transients test more than steady points, and the imposed or tuned inputs determine which outputs are real checks.
Discretisation can decide the answer: with phase change, an end-point exchanger model can remove the optimum being studied.

playbooks.title: Consequence analysis and quantitative risk assessment with integral tools
playbooks.intro: The usual chain is scenario list, hole size or release type, source term, consequence model, then frequencies, ignition, weather and population in a risk integrator. The read works show where results move.

points.text: Analyst and method choices cause large spread: in a benchmark where teams assessed the same facility, frequency estimates still differed by orders of magnitude after site assumptions were aligned. Publish scenario definitions, pipe lengths, use factors, failure data and source-term averaging.
The risk integrator is itself a source of difference: with identical frequencies and consequences, tools still gave different risk results. It can be tested separately with fixed footprints.
Regulatory method, representative substance, ignition probability and software version all change contours, so record them with every result.
With matched inputs, different dense-gas packages can still change distances and the individual risk curve. Name the package and version and check decision distances with a second model.
Frequency effort belongs on the events that set the risk contour, which need not be those with the longest consequence range.
Uncertainty can be reported as a percentile band using a two-loop sampling design, with the location of exposed people treated as part of the scenario.
Check that each generic hole size is physically possible for the equipment, and that the tool's printed inputs match the stated scenario.

Comparisons with experiments are mixed and depend on tool, quantity and averaging rule: hydrogen and propane jet works report both over- and under-prediction, and dense-gas scores depend on segment and averaging choices.

playbooks.title: CFD studies of dispersion, ventilation, fire and explosion
playbooks.intro: The model is built from geometry, a source description, mesh, turbulence and combustion settings and boundary conditions; several of these are first-order choices.

points.text: The leak source is a modelling decision in its own right: expanded-jet sizing of the leak cell, local refinement, roughness and wind speed change the answer for jets and dense clouds.
Turbulence and near-wall settings can dominate low-momentum buoyant leaks in small enclosures.

Validate the quantity the risk study uses. One offshore study validates and tests cloud volume, including its sensitivity to the concentration threshold and the scaling used to reuse one simulation for other cases.
Detector and ventilation studies derive an acceptance cloud size from consequences first; changing fuel changes that criterion as well as the dispersion.
Fire studies check both the physical and the grid non-dimensional numbers against the validation envelope, and test grid effects on every output used.
Prescribed inputs can make a comparison circular, and a coupled predictive sub-model is not automatically better than a prescribed one. Check surface heat feedback and independent measurements.
A design rule fitted to a solver that omits a pressure-raising mechanism rests on removing that mechanism in practice; show validation points one by one.
Parameters tuned on a test weaken that test as validation, so keep calibration and validation cases apart.

playbooks.title: Process flowsheet and equation-oriented models
playbooks.intro: These supply the stream and equipment data that safety studies build on, so their errors carry forward.

points.text: Property methods are a main risk: a default cubic equation of state converged but was badly wrong for a reactive molten feed, and good binary fits did not make a flowsheet reliable for supercritical components.
Real composition and phase envelope should be checked before simplifying a stream that feeds dispersion work.
In equation-oriented work, initialisation is part of the model, and fitted data should be reported separately from validation data.
A parameter tuned on a data set makes comparison with that set calibration, not validation.
Say which part of a flowsheet the data test. Validated sub-models or one validated stage do not validate the integrated process.
Switching from a rate-based steady-state model to an equilibrium dynamic one needs checks across the disturbance range, not only at the design point.
Code-to-code benchmarks need matched property options and component data, and should report non-converged cases. Agreement between simulators is not agreement with a plant.

playbooks.title: How far to trust a result: evaluation protocols, blind tests and users
playbooks.intro: Method guidance and benchmark works describe how a model's credibility is established for a stated use.

points.text: Evaluation protocols compare predictions with listed experiments using stated measures and acceptance ranges. A pass applies to the grid, source model and boundary treatment tested.
Passing statistics are not sufficient on their own: rerun decision-relevant example cases for each model version, since hazard ranges can move.
State whether predictions were blind, report point-wise and arc-wise scores separately, and flag runs outside a model's stated applicability.
Users matter: analysts using the same CFD code, and teams using their own tools on one vented-explosion or risk problem, produced widely different answers.
Fire-model guidance expresses accuracy as bias and scatter for each output quantity within a stated validated range, with a rule for parameters outside it.
For plant models, agree the acceptance band from measurement variability before tuning, and keep data used for correction apart from data used to test.

profiles.title: Determination of Alarm Safety Response Time
profiles.institution_or_venue: IChemE Hazards 26, Symposium Series 161 (Amec Foster Wheeler)
profiles.read_scope: Full text; figure and table images were not readable in the saved text
profiles.objective: Describe how process safety time for alarms and safety instrumented functions is estimated by hand and then confirmed with dynamic simulation, applied to a para-xylene plant column.

tools.name: Aspen HYSYS Dynamics
tools.role: Confirmed and adjusted hand-calculated PST for hazard scenarios.

build_steps.step: Take hazard scenarios needing protective functions from the SIL/LOPA reviews.
First estimate PST as the margin between alarm set point and the hazardous value divided by an estimated rate of change from mass or energy balance.

Simulate each scenario from steady state, including equipment, pipelines and shutdown valves, by applying the scenario's disturbance (for low sump level, feed stopped together with a failed level transmitter).
Record the PST for each scenario in the instrument database and cause-and-effect matrix and use it for SIF response time.
Use PST in alarm classification to test whether an alarm can be credited and to set its priority.

key_choices.value: Where the true failure condition is uncertain, the equipment design limit is assumed.
In the applied cases PST runs from the alarm set point to the equipment or inventory limit.
A minimum of the order of 20-30 min for a safety alarm layer, attributed by the authors to EEMUA 191.

profiles.tool_chain: SIL/LOPA scenarios feed a hand estimate, then HYSYS Dynamics, then the instrument database, cause-and-effect matrix and alarm rationalisation.

validation.detail: The hand estimate is said to be reaffirmed and adjusted by simulation; no numerical comparison is given in the text.

sensitivity.detail: None found in the text.

profiles.lesson: Define PST start and end points explicitly: this paper quotes a standard definition starting at the initiating failure but measures from the alarm set point.
profiles.caveats: Numerical PST results are in figures and tables that did not extract. The 20-30 minute operator-time criterion should be checked against the guideline itself, which was not read here; another paper in this set (harun-2021) cites 10 minutes from the same guideline. The editions cited are BS EN 61511 (2004) and EEMUA 191 (2007).

profiles.title: Advanced Process Modeling and Optimization of Amine-Based Carbon Capture Process
profiles.read_scope: abstract, sections 1.3, 2.2, 2.7-2.9 (parts), 5.1-5.2 (packed column, validation, exchanger), 6.2-6.7 (parts), chapter 7; transport and two-film chapters not read in detail
profiles.objective: Build equation-oriented, rate-based unit models and a thermodynamic sub-model for MEA CO2 capture in IDAES, validate them against pilot data, and optimise a reference plant at part load.

tools.name: IDAES
tools.role: Platform for the column, exchanger, reboiler and condenser models and the plant-wide optimisation.

tools.name: IPOPT
tools.role: Solved the discretised packed-bed equations.

tools.name: Parmest (Pyomo)
tools.role: Regressed thermodynamic parameters from experimental data.

build_steps.step: Regress standard-state and ion-pair/water interaction parameters from selected vapour-liquid equilibrium and heat-of-absorption data before building the columns.
Screen published binary parameter sets with thermodynamic consistency tests before adopting one.
Discretise each packed bed along its height and solve the differential-algebraic system simultaneously.
Initialise in stages: mass balances first, then switch on mass transfer and then heat transfer with continuation parameters.
Fit exchanger heat-transfer parameters on one subset of pilot runs and validate on the rest.
Use the validated unit models for steady-state plant-wide optimisation of part load and variable capture.

key_choices.value: Second-virial-coefficient truncated virial equation, chosen as single-root and adequate at low to moderate pressure.
Symmetric electrolyte-NRTL with a reformulated parameter structure to remove a singularity when ions are absent.
Two reversible reactions represent CO2-loaded MEA chemistry, following Morgan et al. (2017).
Pyomo DAE finite difference with 20 finite elements for the packed bed model.

profiles.tool_chain: Parmest regression feeds the property package; property, transport and hydraulic sub-models feed IDAES unit models; those are assembled into the plant model solved and optimised with IPOPT.

validation.detail: Absorber capture compared with NCCC pilot runs (seven cases in the table; the author cites a largest deviation of 4% of CO2 capture against gas-side data), temperature profiles against NCCC and TCM 2015 baseline data (rich loading absolute percentage deviation 4.1% for the TCM run), and plate exchanger duty with 4% error.

sensitivity.detail: The part-load chapter varies L/G, capture rate and load in optimisation; no formal parametric uncertainty analysis of the column validation was found in the sections read.

limitations.text: The explicit two-film (second generation) column model still has numerical problems that limit industrial use.
Measurement and model uncertainty were not included in the validation comparison.
Validation of the stage-wise column with dynamic data is left to future work.

profiles.lesson: In an equation-oriented model, design the initialisation sequence as part of the model, and report which data were used for fitting and which for validation.
profiles.caveats: The text states a largest absorber deviation of 4% of CO2 capture against gas-side data, while Table 18 lists case 5 as 67.60 predicted against 59.03 gas-side (58.89 liquid-side); how the 4% was calculated is not stated there. IDAES version not stated.

profiles.title: Evaluation of an Open-source Chemical Process Simulator Using a Plant-wide Oil and Gas Separation Plant Flowsheet Model as Basis
profiles.read_scope: whole paper
profiles.objective: Rebuild a published HYSYS oil and gas separation plant model in DWSIM and compare the two at one operating point and over randomly sampled conditions.

tools.name: DWSIM
tools.role: Rebuilt plant-wide flowsheet.

tools.name: Aspen HYSYS
tools.role: Reference commercial simulator.

tools.name: Python wrapper with Latin hypercube sampling
tools.role: Ran the same sampling plan in both simulators.

build_steps.step: Align thermodynamic options to what both tools support before comparing, changing the reference setup if needed.
Enter the same externally estimated pseudo-component properties in both models instead of relying on DWSIM's built-in estimation.
Compare fluid characterisation and phase envelope first, then product streams, driver duties, compressor temperatures and exchanger duties.
Check that recycle mass-balance errors are small enough not to explain differences.
Run a Latin hypercube parametric study over 10 independent variables and report unconverged cases.

key_choices.value: Peng-Robinson, with liquid density and departure functions from the equation of state.
Pseudo-components specified by molecular weight and liquid density, with critical properties and acentric factor estimated by Twu methods.

profiles.tool_chain: A Python wrapper drives both simulators with the same sampling plan; results are compared statistically.

validation.detail: Against HYSYS only. Single point: differences typically below 1%; two exchangers (20-HA-03 and 25-HA-01) differ by -5.8% and -3.9% (30 kW and 24 kW). The paper explains the first by its very small temperature difference and says the same of 25-HA-02. Parametric study: 9 of 100 samples did not converge in DWSIM; R-squared at least 0.99 for liquid flow, power and Reid vapour pressure.

sensitivity.detail: 100 Latin hypercube samples over 10 variables, 91 converged.

limitations.text: DWSIM solved only 91% of the defined parametric cases.
The author suggests possible slight instability in phase-split calculation, needing further study.

profiles.lesson: A fair code-to-code benchmark needs matched property options and component data, and should report non-converged and rerun cases as results.
profiles.caveats: Code-to-code agreement is not plant accuracy; no measured data. Some samples with unexpected deviations were manually re-run, which the reader should weigh.

profiles.title: HydDown Documentation, Release 0.50.0 (theory and validation chapters)
profiles.read_scope: introduction/background, parts of theory located by search, chapter 4 validation (most of it)
profiles.objective: Document an open-source Python vessel filling, depressurisation and fire-load model and compare it with experiments and commercial simulators.

tools.name: HydDown
tools.role: lumped vessel filling, discharge and fire calculations

tools.name: CoolProp
tools.role: thermodynamic back end

tools.name: Honeywell UniSim Design (dynamics mode)
tools.role: code-to-code reference for wall conduction and fire heat load

build_steps.step: Use the lumped wall heat balance for steel cylinders and check against 1-D transient conduction that the result does not change.
For lined composite cylinders with very different layer properties, switch to bi-material 1-D transient conduction rather than lumping the properties.
For the nitrogen vessel test, set the orifice discharge coefficient to match the measured pressure before comparing temperatures.
For two-phase fire cases, use the non-equilibrium option with pool-fire heat load and relief-valve cycling.

key_choices.value: Mainly pure substances; the documentation also lists no gas-phase temperature stratification and, by default, no through-wall gradient.
Set or adjusted to match the measured pressure in the nitrogen (0.8) and multi-component scrubber (0.97) tests; the KIT helium case reuses 0.9 from an earlier study.

profiles.tool_chain: CoolProp properties feed the HydDown energy balance, flow-device and heat-transfer routines.

validation.detail: KIT helium composite-tank test: minimum gas temperature 182.3 K simulated against 177.5 K measured (4.8 K difference), with the simulated minimum earlier (about 75 s against 100 s); final gas temperature 237 K simulated against 216 K measured. The author reports that adding an earlier study's thermocouple thermal model improved the predicted time of the measured minimum and the final measured temperature. The document also gives other experimental cases (with weaker final-temperature or timing agreement in places), fire tests and code-to-code comparisons with UniSim.

sensitivity.detail: Wall-model choice checked for steel cases; liner material swapped (polymer to aluminium) to show its effect on gas temperature. No systematic parameter study seen in the parts read.

limitations.text: A very slow hydrogen depressurisation fitted gas temperature less well than fast ones, which the author suggests points to missing detail in heat transfer.
Composite wall properties are uncertain and strongly influence results.
No good Type III discharge dataset with wall layer details was found, so that case is only illustrative.

profiles.lesson: State for each validation case which inputs were fitted (such as discharge coefficient), because pressure agreement is then not evidence; judge the model on minimum and final temperatures and their timing.
profiles.caveats: Developer-written software documentation, not peer reviewed as read; several tank geometries and properties were assumed from similar vessels. The fire heat load table gives an incident heat flux of 100 kW/m2 while the captions of Figures 4.17 and 4.18, as extracted, give 100 W/m2.

profiles.title: Quantifying Safety with a QRA: To Agree on the Results, the Method Should Be Explicit
profiles.read_scope: whole paper
profiles.objective: Explain why QRA tools give different individual and societal risk results, drawn from TNO comparisons made while rebuilding RISKCURVES.

tools.name: RISKCURVES
tools.version: not stated in the body; reference list cites 9.05
tools.role: Rebuilt QRA tool compared with its previous version and other packages.

tools.name: SAFETI-NL
tools.version: not stated in the body; reference list cites 6.54
tools.role: Comparison package.

tools.name: EFFECTS
tools.role: TNO consequence tool that supplies the model chains to RISKCURVES.

build_steps.step: Separate consequence-model differences from risk-integration differences by feeding identical lethality footprints into the risk engine.
Report how a time-varying release is turned into a dispersion source (segments, average rate or representative rate).
Report probits or thresholds for both indoor and outdoor lethality.
Report dominant model parameters and any departure from defaults with a reason.
Report the risk integration discretisation: grid size, steps and interpolation.

key_choices.value: Warns that collapsing a footprint into blocks of effective cloud width can seriously underestimate risk, especially near the source.
Prefers an indoor dose calculation using ventilation rate over the shortcut of 10 percent of outdoor lethality, which can be very optimistic at high dose.

profiles.tool_chain: EFFECTS-style consequence models feed RISKCURVES; externally computed footprints can be injected through a damage definition.

validation.detail: Even with identical frequencies and consequences, risk results differed between tools. For toxic individual risk, differences of the order of 50 percent were found, mostly at short range.

sensitivity.detail: Qualitative discussion with illustrative figures.

limitations.text: Current guidelines leave too many degrees of freedom and the internal calculation method and resolution are often unclear.

profiles.lesson: Verify a risk-integration engine separately from the consequence models, using fixed footprints. This is directly reusable as a test design for open QRA code.
profiles.caveats: Written by the developer of one of the compared tools. No tabulated comparison data or case definition, so the quoted differences cannot be reproduced from the paper. The paper also cites a Belgian tank-park benchmark with larger differences (stated as up to 400 percent); it is second-hand.

profiles.title: Experimental methods in chemical engineering - Validation of steady-state simulation
profiles.institution_or_venue: Canadian Journal of Chemical Engineering (CC BY; Polytechnique Montreal repository copy)
profiles.read_scope: abstract, parts of the theory section (process data, reconciliation, technique classification), the Kraft mill case study and conclusions; two-column layout
profiles.objective: Set out how to validate steady-state simulations against plant data and operator expectations, illustrated on a Kraft pulp mill washing department.

tools.name: CADSIM Plus
tools.role: Case-study steady-state simulation of the washing department.

tools.name: EXPLORE (CanmetENERGY)
tools.role: Cleaned one year of plant data.

build_steps.step: Remove errors, shutdowns and unsteady periods from historical data before using it.
First verify with operators that major equipment is present and correctly connected.
Run informal (face) validation by consulting several operators one at a time on whether the model is realistic.
Follow with sensitivity analysis (one-at-a-time, then multi-variable) as formal validation of how inputs and parameters move the outputs.
Aim for simulated values within one standard deviation of measurement variability.

key_choices.value: Ten-minute averages over one year of operation.
Most common regime (mode) and a best-performance stable period.

profiles.tool_chain: Cleaned historian data set the inputs and the comparison statistics; expert feedback and sensitivity runs drive model corrections.

validation.detail: Washing department case: five variables compared; authors report all simulated values within one standard deviation of the treated data after validation. An error in a knotter parameter was found during informal validation.

sensitivity.detail: One-at-a-time then multi-variable analysis as the formal validation step.

limitations.text: Measurements covered only part of the flowsheet (24 measurements for 95 streams), so informal validation was needed.
Weekly weighed knotter reject data are less reliable than the frequent averaged measurements.

profiles.lesson: Agree the acceptance band from measured variability before tuning, and report separately the data used to correct the model and data held back to test it.
profiles.caveats: Simulation results that fell outside expected ranges (treated data and expert ranges) led to model modifications, and the final values are judged against the treated data; no separate hold-out data set is described. Software versions appear only in the reference list.

profiles.title: Potential impact of accidental releases of hazardous gases on the immediate habitability of a nuclear power plant
profiles.read_scope: chapter 4 methodology, chapter 5 results, chapter 6 conclusions and recommendations; contents of chapter 3
profiles.objective: Estimate worst-case toxic and flammable consequences for a nuclear plant control room from chlorine, aqueous ammonia and pipeline methane releases.

tools.name: ALOHA
tools.role: Toxic dispersion with indoor concentration, jet-fire radiation and vapour cloud overpressure.

tools.name: SLAB
tools.role: Cross-check of the chlorine dense-gas result only.

build_steps.step: Choose one substance for each behaviour class: neutrally buoyant, dense and flammable.
Define a worst case for each: the whole content of the largest container or pipe, with a ten-minute release assumed.
Apply regulatory worst-case weather (class F, 1.5 m/s).
Model the aqueous ammonia as an evaporating pool giving a neutrally buoyant plume, not as a dense two-phase release.
Compare outdoor and indoor concentrations at the control room using an assumed air-change rate.
For SLAB, derive the extra inputs it needs (liquid fraction, release temperature, source area) outside the code.

key_choices.item: toxic endpoints in the method chapter
key_choices.value: 200 ppm ammonia, 3 ppm chlorine and 50 000 ppm methane regardless of exposure time (the results use AEGL tiers).
Urban value of 100 cm for a site with many obstacles, following US EPA guidance.
Flat; complex terrain ignored.

profiles.tool_chain: The release opening diameter taken from the ALOHA source model was used to set up the SLAB source.

validation.detail: Chlorine concentrations from SLAB and ALOHA at four distances are tabulated; the author judges them comparable and adequate for screening or emergency planning. Thermal radiation distances from ALOHA are also compared with hand calculations. No experimental comparison.

sensitivity.detail: Not performed; recommended as future work.

limitations.text: SLAB has no source-term model, which the author offers as a possible cause of the differences from ALOHA.
ALOHA does not predict fragment trajectories from a blast or their effect on people.

profiles.lesson: Keep one scenario input table and check every tool printout against it. A printout that does not match the stated scenario invalidates the result even if the plots look plausible.
profiles.caveats: Master's mini-dissertation. The methane source input table (Table 4-10) gives 26 bar and a 300 mm pipe, while the ALOHA printout shows 257 atmospheres and a 30-inch pipe. The indoor chlorine concentration is given as 27 ppm in one sentence of the results text and 24.7 ppm elsewhere in the text, table and printout. For the 2 kW/m2 zone the results text gives 243 m, while Table 5-4 and the printout give 700 m. The results text calls 5 000 ppm the lower flammability limit, while the printout lists LEL as 50 000 ppm and labels 5 000 ppm as 10% LEL. Tool versions not stated. Consequence only, no frequencies. DEGADIS is reviewed but not run.

profiles.title: Modelagem e simulacao de uma unidade industrial de producao de acido sulfurico integrada a uma planta de geracao de energia eletrica
profiles.read_scope: abstract, section 3.2 (model development), sections 4.1-4.5 (key parts) and chapter 5 conclusions; in Portuguese
profiles.objective: Simulate an industrial sulfuric acid plant with integrated power generation, comparing the free COCO simulator and UniSim against design data and some operating data.

tools.name: UniSim Design
tools.role: Simulated all circuits including turbines, converter, sulfur furnace and absorbers.

tools.name: COCO Simulator
tools.role: Parallel model of turbines, converter and gas-steam circuits.

tools.name: Maple
tools.role: Independent stoichiometric energy and material balance of the sulfur furnace to judge the simulator.

build_steps.step: Back-calculate turbine section isentropic efficiencies from the energy balance, treating an extraction turbine as two turbines in series.
Represent each catalyst pass as an adiabatic equilibrium reactor and compare outlet temperature and conversion with design values pass by pass.
Integrate gas and steam circuits only after the converter model has been checked, simplifying the economisers to one exchanger with fixed duty.
Test several symmetric and asymmetric property configurations for the sulfur furnace and build an independent hand-style model as reference.
Model the absorption towers as adiabatic equilibrium reactors when no suitable absorber thermodynamics is available.

key_choices.value: ASME Steam in UniSim, preferred over IF-97 for accuracy and wider range.
Peng-Robinson; switching to ideal gas made no difference at the low pressure and high temperature involved.
Peng-Robinson gas with UNIFAC liquid, selected because it gave the smallest furnace errors.
Library sulfur at 150 degrees C chosen as closest to operating temperature.

profiles.tool_chain: Checked turbine and converter sub-models are connected into integrated gas and steam circuits; superheater predictions then set turbine power. Maple serves as a separate reference for the furnace.

validation.detail: Compared mainly with plant design values, plus December 2020 operating values for turbine power. SO2 conversion: authors give a maximum relative error of 3.1%. Integrated gas and steam circuit: largest temperature error, for extraction steam, 15.26% in UniSim and 7.56% in COCO; turbine power about 6% high in UniSim and 1 to 2.5% high in COCO. Furnace outlet temperature: all-Peng-Robinson 19.1% below design, Peng-Robinson gas with UNIFAC liquid 9.5% above, Maple model 0.3%. Absorbers: simulated outlet gas temperatures 102.3 and 98.5 degrees C against 82.0 in design.

sensitivity.detail: Thermodynamic-package sensitivity for the converter and sulfur furnace.

limitations.text: Turbine efficiency variation with steam flow was not modelled, which matters at reduced capacity.
Absorber differences come mainly from the equilibrium-reactor simplification, with no mass transfer along the packing.
The author concludes UniSim is not suitable for liquid sulfur combustion without first adjusting thermodynamic parameters.

profiles.lesson: A default cubic equation of state for both phases can converge and still be badly wrong for a reactive molten feed; keep an independent energy balance for any high-temperature unit.
profiles.caveats: Most comparisons are against design-basis values rather than measurements. The UniSim furnace error is 9.5% in the abstract and 9.6% in the conclusions. The Portuguese summary gives divergences of up to 6.7% for the integrated steam and gas circuit, while Table 17 lists a maximum of 15.26% (extraction steam, UniSim). Text is in Portuguese.

profiles.title: Jack Rabbit II Inter-model Comparison Exercise
profiles.read_scope: all slides as extracted text, including backup input and statistics slides; figures not viewed
profiles.objective: Compare 17 dense-gas dispersion models, including PHAST, ALOHA and SLAB, with three Jack Rabbit II large chlorine release trials.

tools.name: PHAST
tools.role: Run by DNV GL as one of the participating models.

tools.name: ALOHA and SLAB-R
tools.role: Run by RAND as participating models.

build_steps.step: Choose a trial subset and exclude near-field sensors affected by the mock urban array.
Issue common recommended inputs for source, roughness and meteorology, while letting modellers use their own source model.
Request the same outputs from every model: arc maxima at fixed distances, cloud widths and heights, contours and time series.
Keep saturated sensor readings but flag them, since true concentrations were probably higher.
Score with geometric mean bias, geometric variance and factor-of-two and factor-of-five fractions on the closest arcs.

key_choices.value: Two alternative recommended source terms were tabulated: a single constant primary release, or a primary release modified for rainout plus a secondary release from evaporating rainout.
0.5 mm for the playa in the recommended inputs.

profiles.tool_chain: Each participant ran their own model from the shared input sheet.

validation.detail: Model predictions of arc maximum concentration spread over about 1 to 1.5 orders of magnitude, with observations always inside the range. On average widths were over-predicted and heights under-predicted, with cross-sectional area unbiased. The authors name ESCAPE, HPAC and IDDM as apparently better performers.

sensitivity.detail: Not a sensitivity study.

limitations.text: Participants were not on equal footing because some had helped plan the trials and had seen the data.
Real accidents add uncertainty beyond this exercise: unknown source terms, unclear surface deposition and uncertain health effects.
Many models do not represent the obstacle array.

profiles.lesson: For a dense-gas screening code, publish MG, VG and FAC2 on this common input set and expect inter-model spread of an order of magnitude. Hand-picking one tool does not remove that uncertainty.
profiles.caveats: Slide deck, three trials only, with emission estimates marked as still subject to change; the saved text says nothing about peer review. Per-model scores are in a table whose text layout is partly broken in extraction, so they are not repeated here; read the original slide before citing a number for one model. DEGADIS is not among the models listed.

profiles.title: Application of FLACS to develop a standard for explosion venting of empty vessels
profiles.institution_or_venue: University of Stavanger (external supervisor from Gexcon)
profiles.read_scope: abstract, software description and stated limitations, chapter 4 (validation and grid sensitivity), simulation set-up in chapter 5, conclusion, chapter 6 experiment comparison and appendix Table 10
profiles.objective: Use many FLACS vented-explosion runs in empty cubical enclosures to propose a modified, less conservative vent-area recommendation.

tools.name: FLACS
tools.version: not stated (user manual v10.6 is in the references)
tools.role: All vented and closed-vessel explosion simulations

tools.name: CASD and Flowvis
tools.role: Geometry, scenario and grid pre-processing, and post-processing

build_steps.step: Check vent openings in the porosity field, because grid matching can change the effective vent area.
Compare peak internal and external overpressure with published vented-chamber tests before running the parameter study.
Compare a fixed standard cell size with a size scaled to enclosure dimension, using the deflagration index and flame speed in closed boxes.
Run the matrix over gas type, volume, vent area and then ignition position, two vents and elongation, with monitors inside and outside.
Plot all results against an existing correlation and draw the proposed curve to enclose them.

key_choices.value: 0.05 m, following the recommendation of earlier work cited as Klausen (2016).
0.1 m accepted after a 13 to 18 percent difference in comparison metrics.
Same equivalence ratio for every gas, starting without turbulence.
Pressure relief panel on one front face of each enclosure.

profiles.tool_chain: Validation runs and grid check lead to a parameter matrix whose peak pressures are fitted by a modified empirical vent equation.

validation.detail: Six Harrison and Eyre vented tests: the author calls agreement satisfactory with a 30% margin but notes larger deviations at the quarter-area vent, where tabulated internal-pressure ratios are 0.35 and 0.46. Chapter 6 adds comparisons with Bauwens (propane) and Skjold et al. (hydrogen) tests, described as showing rather similar behaviour; Table 10 gives simulated against measured pressures of 0.09/0.06, 0.086/0.07 and 0.073/0.08 bar for propane and 0.35/0.146, 0.248/0.12 and 0.23/0.19 bar for hydrogen.

sensitivity.detail: Closed-box runs comparing the standard 0.1 m cells with a volume-adjusted size (0.025, 0.04, 0.05 and 0.1 m for 2, 4, 20 and 125 m3, so the two coincide at 125 m3), plus physical variations in ignition position, number of vents and length-to-diameter ratio.

limitations.text: FLACS does not model acoustic instabilities, which can dominate pressure in some vented empty enclosures.
The proposal assumes internal turbulence and acoustics do not affect pressure, so other measures must remove them.

profiles.lesson: A design rule fitted to a solver that omits a pressure-raising mechanism depends on assurance that the mechanism is removed in practice. Show validation points one by one: here two internal-pressure points are under-predicted by more than half.
profiles.caveats: Master's thesis. In Table 2 the similarity index is headed experiment over simulation, but the listed values equal simulation over experiment (for test B3, 286 mbar measured, 271 mbar simulated, index 0.95). Read that way, 3 of the 12 indices (0.35, 0.46 and 0.68) are outside the stated 30% margin, all under-predictions. The Harrison and Eyre validation used 0.05 m cells and the parameter study 0.1 m; the grid check compares two sizes in closed boxes. The author states that any guideline based on the proposal must require measures that remove internal turbulence and acoustic effects.

profiles.title: Physical model of non-adiabatic blowdown of cryo-compressed hydrogen storage tanks
profiles.institution_or_venue: International Journal of Hydrogen Energy 48(90) (Ulster University repository copy)
profiles.read_scope: introduction, experiments, model, calculation assumptions, convergence checks, validation, thermocouple inertia, CFD use, conclusions (figures as text only)
profiles.objective: Build and validate a blowdown model for cryo-compressed hydrogen tanks including heat transfer through tank and discharge pipe walls, and use it as a CFD source term.

tools.name: MATLAB
tools.role: implements the blowdown algorithm

tools.name: CoolProp
tools.role: real-gas hydrogen properties

tools.name: ANSYS Fluent
tools.role: jet dispersion using a volumetric source driven by the blowdown results

build_steps.step: Choose validation tests that span the extremes of initial pressure for each nozzle size and both initial temperatures.
Add heat transfer in the short discharge pipe before an isentropic real nozzle and a notional-nozzle expansion.
Test whether a constant pipe-wall temperature can replace transient wall conduction, weighing accuracy against run time.
Check convergence in time step, wall nodes and solver tolerances.
Fit a discharge coefficient test by test and report the range.
Pass transient notional-nozzle mass, momentum, energy and turbulence terms to CFD as constant-size volumetric sources.

key_choices.value: Helmholtz-energy formulation; the authors state the Abel-Noble equation is not applicable to high-pressure cryogenic storage.
20 wall nodes as an accuracy and run-time compromise.
Fitted per test, optimum values 0.6 to 0.8.

profiles.tool_chain: CoolProp properties feed the MATLAB blowdown model; its transient notional-nozzle results are fitted against time and applied as volumetric sources in Fluent.

validation.detail: PRESLHY tank blowdown tests: tank pressure and temperature reproduced well. The authors also state differences were within experimental accuracy, somewhat larger for the bigger release nozzles, which they link to thermocouple inertia. The discharge coefficient was fitted per test. In the CFD jet comparison, sensors near the nozzle were predicted somewhat colder than measured (possibly sensor inertia), with good agreement further downstream.

sensitivity.detail: Time step, solver tolerance, wall nodes, wall thickness, external heat-transfer coefficient, pipe-wall treatment, discharge coefficient and three model variants (adiabatic versus heat transfer, two equations of state). The CFD source-volume size comparison shown is attributed to earlier work.

limitations.text: For other geometries and scenarios, transient pipe-wall conduction should be solved for accurate estimates.
Closed thermocouples may lag in the fastest blowdowns; open ones respond faster but may be less accurate when cold.
The authors say further research is envisaged to assess validity and applicability for larger hydrogen storages and longer discharge lines once detailed experiments are available.

profiles.lesson: Compare against an adiabatic baseline to show what wall heat transfer changes, and examine thermocouple response before attributing fast-transient temperature error to the model.
profiles.caveats: Small 2.81 L tank; per-test fitted discharge coefficient; pipe-wall initial temperature taken from the experiment; agreement is mostly graphical, with no numerical error metric seen in the parts read.

profiles.title: Assessing the current live fire training structure environment in eThekwini using CFD
profiles.read_scope: abstract, FDS description and limitations, design-fire inputs, section 2.4 (validation range and grid study), conclusions and recommendations
profiles.objective: Use FDS to identify heat, gas-temperature and toxic hazards to trainee firefighters on two floors of an existing training building.

tools.name: Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS)
tools.role: Low-Mach CFD fire simulation of both floors

tools.name: FDS Validation Guide
tools.role: Source of the non-dimensional validation ranges and model uncertainty statistics

build_steps.step: Specify the heat release rate history, fire size and location, fuel chemistry and soot and CO yields as inputs.
Build a validation envelope only from test series that resemble the case, then check the model's own experimental and numerical non-dimensional numbers against it.
Where a parameter falls outside, restrict the output locations rather than extrapolate.
Run a series of cell sizes that all keep the plume resolution index inside the validated range, stepping by 10 mm, and plot the quantities of interest near peak heat release.
Turn predictions into probability of exceeding tenability limits using the published model bias and scatter.

key_choices.value: 110 mm on the ground floor and 70 mm on the first floor.
Wood pallets, with chemical formula, CO and soot yields and heat of combustion tabulated.
Limited so that the training fire does not become ventilation controlled.
Preferred restarting an interrupted run over coarsening the grid.

profiles.tool_chain: A design-fire HRR feeds FDS; device outputs feed tenability and garment exposure calculations with model-uncertainty probabilities.

validation.detail: No comparison of this study's results with measurements. Applicability is argued by showing the case parameters lie within validation-guide ranges; the one exception, a ground-floor distance ratio, was handled by limiting target distance.

sensitivity.detail: Ten cell sizes per floor. A separate comparison showed that CO volume fraction changed far more than temperature or heat flux with coarsening or with restarts.

limitations.text: Results are estimates of what would be measured in real training; the author recommends further validated test series for targets farther from the fire.
Ground-floor target distances had to be restricted to stay within validation.

profiles.lesson: Check both the physics and the grid non-dimensional numbers against the validation envelope, and test grid effects on every output you will use: species such as CO can move far more than temperature.
profiles.caveats: Master's thesis with no fire measurements from this building; being inside a validation-guide parameter range is not a test of this particular model. Section 2.2 calls the tall-stack fire ultra-fast and the short-stack fire medium but gives the same growth coefficient, 0.01172 kW/s2, for both.

profiles.title: Model Evaluation Report on DRIFT Version 3.7.23
profiles.institution_or_venue: UK Health and Safety Executive, Research Report RR1231
profiles.read_scope: key messages, executive summary, sections 1 to 3, 4.1, 4.2, 4.4 to 4.6, 6.1, 6.6 and 7; per-trial validation plots and appendices not read
profiles.objective: Regulator's own evaluation of a new version of the DRIFT dense gas dispersion model against a purpose-built Model Evaluation Protocol before use in its statutory advice.

tools.name: DRIFT
tools.role: Model under evaluation

tools.name: DRIFT (previous version in regulatory use)
tools.role: Baseline for the exemplar scenario comparison

tools.name: LNG Model Validation Database
tools.role: Starting point of the validation database

build_steps.step: Run a scientific assessment by completing a model questionnaire and testing pass/fail qualitative criteria.
Treat verification as evidence gathered from the developer and documentation and record it in the evaluation report.
Assemble a validation database so the regulator can validate independently of the developer, starting from the LNG protocol database and adding passive releases, more substances and jet releases.
Compare arc-wise maximum concentration and cloud width, matching the model averaging time to the experimental one.
Score field and wind-tunnel data separately with statistical performance measures against stated acceptance ranges.
Run a set of exemplar scenarios typical of the real regulatory use in both old and new versions, and explain every significant difference from model physics changes.

key_choices.value: Statistical performance measures and acceptance ranges taken from the LNG protocol applied to all trials, including non-dense ones.
Set to 1 s because the plume meander model does not apply to controlled tunnel inflow.
Some wind-tunnel cases (sloping terrain releases and off-axis sensor sets) were excluded as outside model capability.
Database revision changed inputs and measurements, so scores of older and newer model versions need care.
The quantities used for land-use zones: distances and widths of toxic dose isopleths, and flammable concentration isopleths.

profiles.tool_chain: Questionnaire and qualitative criteria, then developer verification evidence, then validation runs scored by statistical measures, then exemplar runs through a spreadsheet tool that extracts and compares outputs of two model versions.

validation.detail: For field trials all five measures for concentration and cloud width were within the acceptance ranges. For wind-tunnel concentrations DRIFT tended to underpredict and FAC2 was 0.49 against a criterion above 0.5; the other measures passed.

sensitivity.detail: No input sensitivity study in the parts read; version-to-version differences were examined on exemplar scenarios, with the largest ones for the pool component of large refrigerated ammonia releases.

limitations.text: The model handles only flat terrain, with buildings and fences represented as cuboids or rectangles.
The expansion region from liquid storage to a cloud containing solids, as for carbon dioxide, is not modelled.
One added hydrogen fluoride dataset had been used during development, so that comparison is not fully independent.

profiles.lesson: Pass statistics are not enough: also rerun the decision-relevant exemplar cases on every model version, because a version that passes validation can still move hazard ranges substantially.
profiles.caveats: The evaluating organisation is also the model's regulatory user. Verification relies on developer evidence. A significant difference between versions that is explained by physics changes is not thereby shown to be correct.

profiles.title: Use of LOPA and HAZOP Concepts for Complex Automated Hazard Identification
profiles.read_scope: Full paper
profiles.objective: Combine steady-state, bifurcation and dynamic analysis to test, layer by layer, whether process design and basic control contain HAZOP deviations in a propylene glycol CSTR.

tools.name: Own mathematical model (steady-state algebraic and dynamic ODE reactor model with PI control)
tools.role: Solves steady-state branches, bifurcation maps and dynamic deviation responses; the software used is not named in the paper.

build_steps.step: Write the reactor and jacket mass and energy balances as both a steady-state system and a dynamic system.
Plot steady-state solution diagrams for the most influential deviation, with and without controller movement of the manipulated variable.
Build a two-parameter bifurcation map of disturbance variable against manipulated variable that marks stable, oscillating and unstable regions.
Overlay each deviation before and after controller action, then confirm suspect cases with a dynamic run.
Record the results as a HAZOP table with impact, likelihood, risk matrix rank, safeguards and recommendations.

key_choices.value: Taken from the Fogler textbook.
97 degC, above which much of the mixture evaporates.
Proportional-integral controller.

profiles.tool_chain: Steady-state branches feed the bifurcation map, which picks deviations for dynamic runs; results populate the HAZOP table.

sensitivity.detail: Four propylene oxide feed deviations are shown (A +30%, B +66%, C +120%, D -17%). The text says all except A can become dangerous because controller action can move them into oscillating or unstable regions, but also that for B the controller got the system out of the oscillation region. The conclusions name C and D as most hazardous, with process control initiating temperature oscillation.

limitations.text: Once a controller is added, ordinary steady-state diagrams can no longer predict the response because the manipulated variable changes continuously.

profiles.lesson: Credit the control system only after simulating it: for exothermic reactors, test whether controller action itself moves a mild deviation into an unstable regime.
profiles.caveats: Not a commercial simulator study and the solving software is not named. The abstract refers to PID control while section 2.2 describes PI action. No frequency calculation or PFD values are given beyond broad likelihood classes. The statement that all deviations except A can become dangerous through controller action sits beside the statement that for B the controller moved the system out of the oscillation region.

profiles.title: Process Design and Economics for Conversion of Lignocellulosic Biomass to Ethanol: Thermochemical Pathway by Indirect Gasification and Mixed Alcohol Synthesis
profiles.read_scope: section 2.3 (Aspen Plus model), parts of 3.3, 3.4, 3.8-3.9, sections 5-7, Appendix G start
profiles.objective: Document a benchmark process design and economic model for ethanol from woody biomass by indirect gasification and mixed alcohol synthesis, with research targets.

tools.name: Aspen Plus
tools.role: Plant-wide mass and energy balances.

build_steps.step: Represent real species from the component database and treat biomass, ash and char as non-conventional solids.
Assign property packages by plant area rather than using one for the whole plant.
Model complex absorption sub-systems in separate simulations and import their results.
Predict gasifier gas with temperature correlations fitted to pilot data and close char by mass difference.
Set reformer conversions to stated research targets with outlet at shift equilibrium.
Let the model adjust steam-cycle water flow to close the heat balance found by pinch analysis.

key_choices.value: RKS with Boston-Mathias modification for much of the plant.
NRTL with ideal gas for alcohol separation; ASME 1967 steam tables for the steam cycle.
Correlations from a 9 tonne per day pilot facility, mostly 1,500 to 1,672 degrees F.
Kinetic model supplied by Dow under confidentiality, based on bench and pilot data.

profiles.tool_chain: Pilot-data correlations, target reformer conversions, a confidential kinetic model and separate absorber simulations feed one Aspen Plus balance; its results drive pinch analysis, equipment costing and a minimum selling price with sensitivity cases.

validation.detail: Only components are tied to data: gasifier correlations come from pilot runs, and the alcohol kinetic model is shown in parity plots against experiments. The integrated plant is a forward-looking design with no plant validation.

sensitivity.detail: One-parameter and feedstock scenarios on minimum ethanol selling price; less than plus or minus 20% price uncertainty for plus or minus 30% capital cost uncertainty.

limitations.text: Reformer targets were mostly shown at bench scale; continuous pilot operation was still to be demonstrated.
The gasifier and tar reformer were not commercially available.

profiles.lesson: For a plant that does not exist, tabulate which blocks are data correlations, which are targets and which are rigorous, and keep that distinction with every headline result.
profiles.caveats: Conceptual nth-plant design built on future research targets; part of the kinetics is confidential and so not reproducible. Read from a Wayback copy of the NREL PDF. Software version is old.

profiles.title: Operational Safety of the Polymerization Reactors
profiles.institution_or_venue: Instituto Superior Tecnico, Lisbon (internship at SGL Composites)
profiles.read_scope: abstract, objectives, chapter 6 (kinetics and adiabatic test), chapter 7 (Aspen runs and pilot tests), conclusions
profiles.objective: Judge whether runaway or explosion is possible in acrylonitrile copolymerisation reactors under feed, cooling, agitation, pH and inventory deviations, using simulation and pilot tests.

tools.name: Aspen Plus (Polymers template)
tools.role: steady-state sensitivity of reactor temperature to feed-flow deviations

build_steps.step: Take copolymerisation kinetic parameters from handbook and article values and compare the two sources.
Define components, flowsheet, kinetics and industrial inlet conditions, and establish the stationary state.
Vary one feed flow at a time with the sensitivity module and record overflow temperature.
Cover the deviations the simulation did not (cooling, agitation, inerting, pH, unreacted monomer) by pilot-reactor experiments.

key_choices.value: A 12 m3 reactor in simulation; pilot experiments in a 5.7 L reactor with conditions adjusted to suit.
Adiabatic behaviour was approximated by draining the pilot reactor jacket, which the author says is not fully insulated.

profiles.tool_chain: Kinetic data feed the Aspen Plus model; pilot tests are run separately and are not used to calibrate or check the model in the parts read.

validation.detail: No comparison of Aspen predictions with plant or pilot measurements was found in the sections read.

sensitivity.detail: One-at-a-time feed-flow variations in the steady-state model.

limitations.text: Controller lag and operator response are not represented, so real behaviour may differ from the simulation.

profiles.lesson: Steady-state feed-flow sensitivities show operating-point temperature changes only. A runaway assessment also needs transient heat generation against removal, calorimetry and credible loss-of-cooling and agitation cases.
profiles.caveats: Masters thesis; software version not stated. The conclusions say there is no need for concern about explosion or runaway, at least considering the operating procedures, operator training and experience and existing control instrumentation. The same chapter says the cooling-loss, agitation-loss, adiabatic and unreacted-monomer scenarios affect reactor safety and are hard to control, with the mass solidifying within minutes and temperature rising, and that accidents are avoided because the reactor is stopped and cleaned out.

profiles.title: Unpicking Oversimplification: Relief and Flare Studies for Complex Plant using Dynamic Process Modelling
profiles.institution_or_venue: IChemE Hazards 26, Symposium Series No 161 (Flexible Process Consultants Ltd)
profiles.read_scope: whole paper (figures as text only)
profiles.objective: Describe an auditable procedure for a plant-wide dynamic relief and flare study of a legacy refinery covering two flare systems, to check relief devices and header capacity.

tools.name: dynamic process simulator (product used not identified)
tools.role: linked unit models run through relief, utility-failure and operator-error scenarios; the paper names Dynsim, HYSYS, UniSim and gPROMS only as available tools

build_steps.step: Collect deeper equipment data than a conventional relief study (tray and exchanger geometry, valve trim, actuator speeds), mark it up and have a second engineer check the inputs.
Treat historian data as distributions rather than one snapshot, to find realistic worst-case operating states.
Build the steady-state model first, then the dynamic model, then several initial conditions, and review them with plant engineers.
Rate the model against plant data and resolve each discrepancy with site process engineers; use site controller schemes and tunings.
Build each scenario from initiating event, initial condition and optional latent failure, and run it through scripted events so it is repeatable.
Do sensitivity runs on initial conditions, controller modes and latent failures to find the worst credible case, and report each event as a narrative plus peaks and trends.

key_choices.value: One per scenario for unit cases where possible, to add conservatism without double jeopardy; one per major operating unit for site-wide events.
Unit cases put controllers in manual and take no operator action, run for at least 30 simulated minutes unless steady; site-wide cases let realistic controllers act.
Unit models linked through shared utilities and headers (fuel gas, flare, heat integration) so knock-on relief loads appear.

profiles.tool_chain: Plant data and P&ID-derived PFD feed a steady-state model, then a rated dynamic model, then scripted scenarios; slug-flow results were passed to a mechanical model and results supported HAZOP, LOPA and SIL work.

validation.detail: The method requires rating the models so that temperatures, pressures, compositions and valve positions sit within the normal historical range, and says the study's units were rated and matched to plant data. No numerical agreement is reported and no relief transient is compared with measurement in a quantified way.

sensitivity.detail: Described as part of the method; one high-pressure to low-pressure separator example shows that initial liquid levels change the relief case from vapour to two-phase.

limitations.text: The author notes the standard gives little guidance on dynamic modelling studies, so the team had to define its own practice.
A single plant snapshot can be unrepresentative (unusual settings, fouling, bad instruments, ambient or transient conditions).

profiles.lesson: For brownfield flare studies, rate the model on historian distributions and script every scenario with a stated latent-failure and controller-credit rule, so reviewers can challenge the assumptions behind the load.
profiles.caveats: Consultancy conference paper reporting its own project; software product, thermodynamics and flare hydraulics not described; claimed savings are not independently checked.

profiles.title: Investigation of Co-Current and Counter-Current Multiphase Flow in Upstream Drilling and Production Applications
profiles.read_scope: abstract, chapter 2 methodology and results (to the small-scale experiments), chapter 3 equations and data fit, section 3.7 and chapter 4
profiles.objective: Use transient 1-D simulation, with small-scale visual experiments, to study gas removal during bullheading well kill and the operating window of liquid-assisted gas lift.

tools.name: OLGA
tools.role: Transient multiphase simulation of both well operations.

build_steps.step: Reduce the real annulus-tubing well to two vertical pipes joined by a near-lossless check valve, which also stabilises the numerics.
Set geometry, fluids, back pressure and thermal boundary conditions from a published large-scale experiment.
History-match pressure traces from two shallow-well test cases by tuning pipe roughness and valve discharge coefficient.
Hold the fitted parameters fixed when extrapolating to other shallow and deep well scenarios.
Sweep gas and liquid rates and plot maximum injection pressure and average holdup as contour maps.
Probe an unexpected simulated trend with a dimensionally scaled small-scale experiment.

key_choices.value: 402 cells for the bullheading well: 200 each in annulus and tubing and 2 for the check valve.
Roughness 0.00198 in (0.05 mm) and valve discharge coefficient 0.289.
Peng-Robinson equation of state (as described in chapter 3).
Matching pressure histories at several locations for given rates.

profiles.tool_chain: Published large-scale data set the simulation geometry; the simulated trend motivates a small-scale air-water experiment; in the gas-lift part, history-matched parameters feed scenario sweeps.

validation.detail: Bullheading: the large-scale experiments (4 points) show gas removal rising monotonically with liquid rate, whereas simulation shows an up-down-up trend; small-scale air-water tube tests (6 ft, 1 in) show the up-down-up trend qualitatively. Gas lift: two shallow-well cases history-matched (figures only).

sensitivity.detail: Wide sweeps of gas and liquid injection rates for shallow and deep wells.

limitations.text: The gas-lift study ignores the reservoir.
Further large-scale experiments with other fluids, especially non-Newtonian drilling fluids, are recommended.

profiles.lesson: State separately what the simulator matched, what it contradicted and what was only checked qualitatively at another scale.
profiles.caveats: The Chapter 4 conclusions say the 1-D simulation results fit the large-scale experiments successfully, whereas section 2.5 says the experiments (four points) seem to show gas removal efficiency rising monotonically while the simulation shows an up-down-up trend. The small-scale air-water test is compared with the simulated behaviour only by the shape of the trend. Section 3.4.2 prints vector-form conservation equations that include species-diffusion and reaction-heat terms, while section 2.4 prints one-dimensional phase balances. OLGA version not stated.

profiles.title: Determining safety parameters for small scale passive hydrogen venting schemes (fuel cell and nuclear enclosures)
profiles.read_scope: abstract opening, CFD workflow and statistics (3.9-3.10), CFD approach table, ANSYS Fluent comparison (5.9), helium-hydrogen comparison and CFD discussion in chapter 6, appendix E
profiles.objective: Find passive vent arrangements that keep a small fuel-cell enclosure below flammable concentrations, using helium experiments and CFD with two commercial codes.

tools.name: SolidWorks Flow Simulation
tools.role: Main CFD predictions for all vent arrangements

tools.name: ANSYS Fluent
tools.version: 19.2 in the section 3.9.6 heading; the reference list cites 18.2
tools.role: Second code, tested with several RANS, LES and DES settings on one cross-flow case

build_steps.step: Run helium release tests as a hydrogen analogue for the vent arrangements, then simulate them in CFD.
Extend the CFD domain to the outer enclosure of the test rig and refine locally around plume, stratified layer and vents.
Test at least three mesh levels for every ventilation configuration and compare concentration-height profiles.
For the second code, import the same CAD geometry, extract the fluid volume, use a symmetry half-model and sweep turbulence and wall treatments.
Score predictions with fractional bias, normalised mean square error and geometric mean statistics.
In CFD, repeat the cross-flow case with hydrogen in place of helium to test the analogue.

key_choices.value: k-epsilon variant with damping functions in SolidWorks Flow Simulation.
511363 cells on a symmetry half-model.
Refined to a 6.1 million cell equivalent small domain, which gave close agreement for the four further variants shown.
Pressure outlets.

profiles.tool_chain: Helium experiments provide profiles for both codes; the SolidWorks CAD model is reused in Fluent; helium and hydrogen runs are then compared.

validation.detail: Helium concentration profiles in the test enclosure. The author found no Fluent RANS configuration closely matched the cross-flow case, while SolidWorks did well on peak and layer depth and refined LES/DES settings correlated very well.

sensitivity.detail: Mesh levels per configuration; in an example, the coarse mesh under-predicted and well-refined meshes over-predicted stratified layer depth. Turbulence models and wall treatments were swept in Fluent.

limitations.text: Complex or finer meshes often exceeded the available computing capacity.
The domain matched the rig's outer enclosure; a larger one might have helped but was costly.

profiles.lesson: For low-momentum buoyant leaks in small enclosures, treat turbulence and near-wall settings as first-order uncertainties: two commercial codes and several k-epsilon variants can disagree widely on stratification.
profiles.caveats: Chapter 5 says fine meshes were chosen in all instances, while the chapter 6 mesh example says the coarse mesh under-predicted and the well-refined meshes over-predicted stratified-layer depth, with a medium mesh predicting well on that occasion; agreement at one mesh level does not show grid independence. The Fluent study covers one case and includes LES runs with a symmetry plane, which the author says is not generally recommended for LES. SolidWorks training and software access were funded by the industrial collaborator BOC Ltd.

profiles.title: The benefits of using CFD for designing gas detection systems
profiles.read_scope: methodology, explosion, ventilation and dispersion studies, most of the results and the conclusions
profiles.objective: Compare gas detector layouts on two bridge-linked offshore platforms against a large set of simulated leaks, with the danger criterion set from explosion loads on the drilling platform and from gas concentration at target buildings on the production platform.

tools.name: FLACS
tools.role: Explosion, ventilation and dispersion simulations

build_steps.step: Model geometry as completely as possible, since missing detail is a main error source.
Run explosions over cloud size, position and ignition points to find the smallest cloud exceeding target design loads.
Run ventilation for eight wind directions to find air change rates and flow patterns.
Choose leak positions, directions, rates and winds that give clouds both significant and hard to detect, using the flow patterns.
Score each detector layout on fraction detected, time to alarm and detection before the dangerous volume or building impairment.

key_choices.value: 1.5, 6, 24 and 96 kg/s, including sonic jets and low-momentum diffusive leaks.
Calm, 4.8, 8 and 14.9 m/s.
Air change rate assumed linear in wind speed.
Worst-case, challenging scenarios; no frequency or risk weighting.
264 m3, from explosion loads against design accidental loads.

profiles.tool_chain: Explosion runs set the dangerous-cloud criterion; ventilation runs guide leak and detector choice; transient dispersion monitor histories are used to score detector layouts.

validation.detail: No comparison with measurements is presented for this study.

sensitivity.detail: Many scenario and layout variants, but no grid or model-setting sensitivity is reported.

limitations.text: The study was not risk based: leak frequencies and wind probability were not used.

profiles.lesson: Derive the cloud size that detectors must catch from consequences, and report detection-before-impairment, not just detection: a layout can look good on the second measure and fail the first.
profiles.caveats: Case study authored by the FLACS vendor. Grid, source-term set-up and validation were not found in the paper. The drilling-platform results text mentions 336 leak scenarios (also the stated number of explosion runs) and the conclusions give 304 drilling and 224 production dispersion runs; the stated total of 560 equals 336 plus 224, not 304 plus 224.

profiles.title: Modelling and Validation of CO2 Capture Processes with Piperazine
authors: Mariana Rodrigues Ferreira de Sousa Gomes
profiles.institution_or_venue: Universidade do Porto, with Process Systems Enterprise
profiles.read_scope: abstract, chapters 3, 4, 5.1 and 7
profiles.objective: Extend a vendor capture model library to piperazine solvent, validate the absorber against pilot data and compare and optimise process configurations.

tools.name: gPROMS ModelBuilder
tools.role: Flowsheet simulation and optimisation.

tools.name: gCCS capture library
tools.role: Rate-based two-film column and auxiliary unit models.

tools.name: gSAFT
tools.role: Physical property package for gas and liquid.

build_steps.step: Add missing solvent transport property correlations to the library, checking how much the results depend on poorly known ones.
Choose a fitted viscosity form that stays physical outside the measured temperature range.
Initialise columns at an easy condition, save the solution, then move inputs to the target in small steps.
Tune the solvent diffusivity multiplier to reduce CO2 removal deviation against pilot runs.
Solve the stripper loop open first, then close recycles with recycle-breaker blocks once outlets match inlets.
Compare configurations with the same lean solvent, flue gas and utility conditions.

key_choices.value: SAFT-VR based package that treats CO2-amine reaction implicitly as association, avoiding explicit ionic species.
Two-film, distributed axially, films not discretised, reactions only in the liquid bulk, equilibrium at the interface.
Mellapak 250Y used because data for the pilot packing were not available to the author.
Flue gas assumed water saturated, as only CO2 content was reported.

profiles.tool_chain: Validated absorber (and an intercooled version) is placed into five full capture flowsheets, which are then subjected to sensitivity analysis and gPROMS optimisation.

validation.detail: University of Texas pilot absorber, 15 runs plus 2 intercooled runs. CO2 removal deviations in the printed table reach -13% (run 1); the abstract and conclusions state a maximum of -12%. Rich loading deviations are much smaller. The diffusivity factor was adjusted against these removal data.

sensitivity.detail: Intercooling temperature and position, stripper pressure, L/G and piperazine concentration; surface tension checked and found minor.

limitations.text: Column and flash models only initialise within a narrow range far from operating conditions, making initialisation very time consuming.
Diffusivity data for piperazine are scarce, so values were adjusted toward experimental results.
The stripper could not be defined from the pilot data beyond its pressure.

profiles.lesson: If a parameter is tuned on a data set, call the comparison with that set calibration, and keep independent runs for validation.
profiles.caveats: The calibration and validation data overlap, although the author calls the model predictive. Maximum deviation text (-12%) disagrees with the table (-13%). Later chapters call the stripper validated although the validation chapter gives no stripper comparison. Several numbers are missing from the extracted text.

profiles.title: Evaluation of CFD modelling of gas dispersion near buildings and complex terrain
profiles.institution_or_venue: IChemE Symposium Series No. 144; WS Atkins Safety and Reliability
profiles.read_scope: whole paper
profiles.objective: Report how much CFD dispersion results vary with the way the same code is applied by four organisations, and their accuracy against wind-tunnel data, plus a complex-terrain chlorine application.

tools.name: STAR-CD
tools.role: Main CFD code, shared by the four partners for the cases it covered

tools.name: ADREA-HF
tools.role: Second CFD code, developed for atmospheric dispersion

tools.name: HGSYSTEM
tools.version: not stated in the text body (reference list cites the 3.0 manual)
tools.role: Simple-model comparison, scoping and two-phase jet source for the site study

build_steps.step: Isolate user effect by having all partners use the same CFD code for each test case.
Invent new test geometries and run them blind, without access to the wind-tunnel data.
Compare partners qualitatively, on hazard-relevant cloud quantities, with point-based geometric bias and variance, and against a simple model.
For the complex-terrain site, work in stages: simple-model scoping, flat-terrain CFD, coarse far-field terrain model, then a finer near-field model with buildings.
Convert the two-phase jet to a pure vapour source in CFD at the point where little aerosol remains.

key_choices.value: Each modeller used own or published domain rules with no consensus; mesh design and numerics were a main cause of variability.
Changing the k-epsilon model in STAR-CD had little effect, but switching ADREA-HF to k-epsilon could double a hazard range.
Treated as fundamental; variability was greatest for large instantaneous releases with uncertain initial cloud.
Velocity profiles were similar across partners but turbulence profiles differed considerably, some unrealistically.

profiles.tool_chain: In the site study HGSYSTEM scoping and jet calculations provide a vapour source with entrainment sinks to the CFD; a coarse far-field terrain run was meant to give boundary conditions to the near-field run, which proved difficult and was simplified.

validation.detail: Blind comparison with wind-tunnel data for part of the cases. Separately, at the 1% source-concentration level the four partners' maximum hazard ranges differed by factors of 1.5 to 5; the authors report STAR-CD hazard ranges tending to exceed experimental values.

sensitivity.detail: Effects of turbulence model, mesh resolution and differencing scheme were observed. Finer meshes and higher-order differencing tended to reduce scatter against experiment, but there was little evidence that large cell counts (about 120k to 180k) were much better than 60k to 80k, and bias depended on the turbulence model.

limitations.text: Mesh-independent solutions were not attainable for practical 3D building-wake dispersion with the computers of the time.
A finer, numerically better solution need not match experiment better, because mesh and turbulence errors can cancel.
In the site study the near-field domains were too small for some transient clouds.

profiles.lesson: Budget for analyst training and independent checking: sign errors, unit conversions, specification reading, mesh rules, source conditions and inlet turbulence all contributed to large differences between analysts using the same CFD code.
profiles.caveats: Short conference overview of a longer 1997 project report. Computing power and codes are dated. The publication year is not printed in the extracted text and is inferred from the symposium series number. Some partners were new to the code, so the measured spread includes learning effects.

profiles.title: Assessment of Operators' Response Time on Safe Operation of Distillation Columns: A Process Dynamic Analysis
profiles.read_scope: Full paper
profiles.objective: Follow up a LOPA on two refinery columns by simulating cooling water and reflux failures to find operator response time and check relief behaviour.

tools.name: iCON-Symmetry
tools.role: Dynamic models of two columns and their overpressure scenarios.

build_steps.step: Take LOPA concerns (relief adequacy and time for operators to isolate) as the questions for the dynamic study.
Build each column from drawings, datasheets, cause-and-effect matrix, relief load calculations, control valve data and control narratives.
Include equipment sizes, elevations and the control configuration.
Run each event and measure the time from the initiating failure to relief valve opening.
Rerun the worst case with staggered relief valve set pressures to study chattering.

key_choices.value: Advanced Peng-Robinson, chosen for light hydrocarbons.
Structural effects of relief forces were assumed to add no hazard.
The existing high-high pressure alarm was not treated as an independent protection layer.

profiles.tool_chain: LOPA findings define scenarios; plant documents feed the dynamic model; the timings go into updated operating procedures.

validation.detail: Relief valve adequacy from the simulation is said to agree with the relief load calculation documents; no numbers are compared and there is no plant-data validation.

sensitivity.detail: Two columns, two failure types and three relief set-pressure arrangements. In column C-1 cooling water failure all five relief valves opened in about 9 min.

profiles.lesson: Report the time between each alarm, trip and relief event separately. Then ask whether the window left for the operator is realistic before it goes into a procedure or LOPA credit.
profiles.caveats: The updated procedure gives operators two minutes (C-1) and one minute (C-2) after the high-high pressure alarm, while the paper itself cites a 10 minute EEMUA 191 benchmark for acceptable operator response; the authors say control-room operators can quickly push the safety switch, and no human-factors assessment is shown.
