The conclusion that fewer relief valves would suffice rests on the dynamic simulation, with no relief sizing review of it presented. The text gives one Option 1 set point as 10%, while Table 1 lists 22.4 barg for that valve.

profiles.title: Dynamic simulation of Texas City Refinery explosion for safety studies
profiles.institution_or_venue: IChemE Hazards 24, Symposium Series 159 (University of Hull)
profiles.read_scope: Full paper
profiles.objective: Reproduce the raffinate splitter start-up of the 2005 Texas City accident dynamically, then use the model for a more-temperature HAZOP scenario.

tools.name: Aspen HYSYS
tools.role: Dynamic filling and heating of the column.

build_steps.step: Replace the flooded distillation column with a tank separator because no separation was taking place while it filled.
Set vessel liquid volume as column internal volume less the volume taken by internals.
Lump the many feed hydrocarbons into four carbon-number groups from C5 to C8.
Take initial conditions from published investigation data and run the accident timeline in stages as heat input changes.
Rerun with a guide-word deviation plus the failures of the day, and plot it against the reconstructed incident.

key_choices.value: Averaged to 16.3 kg/s because reported rates varied.
More temperature: all four burners lit from 10:00, with the bottom level valve closed.

profiles.tool_chain: Investigation report data build the HYSYS dynamic model, which is then reused for the deviation scenario.

validation.detail: Compared with accident records: simulated liquid level 47.9 m at 1:12 pm against 48 m at 1:02 pm in the CSB report, and temperature said to match another published UniSim simulation closely.

sensitivity.detail: One alternative heat-input scenario; complete feed vaporisation occurred much earlier than on the incident day.

limitations.text: The significance lies in extending the model to dynamic HAZOP rather than in a rigorous reconstruction.
Behaviour downstream of the column was not studied.

profiles.lesson: A deliberately simplified equipment surrogate can be fit for an overfill scenario if you state which phenomena it drops and check level and temperature against records.
profiles.caveats: The year is not printed in the saved text (the page header gives Symposium Series 159, Hazards 24). The level agreement compares a simulated value at 1:12 pm with a reported value at 1:02 pm. The paper notes it has been suggested that the vapour behaviour on the day cannot be accurately predicted by standard tray-separation models in commercial simulators.

profiles.title: Optimal operation of cooling cycle/LNG process
profiles.institution_or_venue: NTNU, Department of Chemical Engineering (external adviser from Norsk Hydro)
profiles.read_scope: abstract, section 2.4, ammonia case study (modelling, optimisation, discussion, conclusions), section 4.3-4.4 and appendix model specifications
profiles.objective: Study degrees of freedom and control of refrigeration cycles in dynamic HYSYS, first for an ammonia cycle and then for a C3-MR LNG process.

tools.name: Aspen HYSYS
tools.role: Steady-state and dynamic models and controller tests.

build_steps.step: Build the steady-state case close to the published reference study to allow comparison.
Do a degrees-of-freedom analysis to allocate valves and compressor work before adding controllers.
Tune controllers from step responses fitted as approximate transfer functions.
Step the optimising valve and allow long settling between steps to locate the optimum in the dynamic model.
Replace the main cryogenic exchanger with shell-and-tube units using the detailed rating model; model most other exchangers with the basic model at first to find approximate UA values.

key_choices.value: Soave-Redlich-Kwong.

key_choices.item: Property package, appendix specifications for C3-MR
key_choices.value: Peng-Robinson.

key_choices.item: Heat exchanger rating model, ammonia cycle
key_choices.value: Detailed zoned model for the condenser and basic UA model for the vaporizer. A run with the basic end-point model on the condenser showed no subcooling optimum.
Fractionation column omitted; main exchanger replaced by shell-and-tube exchangers; multistage compressors split into separate units.

validation.detail: The qualitative conclusion of an earlier modelling study (some condenser subcooling is optimal) is reproduced in dynamic HYSYS; the numerical value differs. No plant data. The C3-MR dynamic model was not completed or validated.

sensitivity.detail: Heat exchanger model fidelity and valve position were varied; the optimum was very flat.

limitations.text: Dynamic mode does not allow an initial liquid level or holdup to be specified in heat exchangers.
Basic end-point exchanger rating should not be used where phase change occurs.
There was not enough time to complete the LNG model in the desired detail.
Unexplained small spikes appeared when superheat reached zero; model or numerical cause unknown.

profiles.lesson: Check that the heat exchanger discretisation can represent the effect you are optimising; with phase change an end-point UA model can remove the optimum entirely.
profiles.caveats: Old software version; diploma work; no data validation. The appendix property statement is read as applying to the C3-MR case because it sits among its model specifications.

profiles.title: Automated Model-based HAZOP Study in Process Hazard Analysis
profiles.read_scope: Full paper
profiles.objective: Present a software tool that generates HAZOP deviations, runs them in a commercial simulator and produces a HAZOP-like report, shown on an ammonia synthesis reactor system.

tools.name: Aspen HYSYS
tools.role: Simulation engine for each deviation.

tools.name: In-house automated HAZOP tool
tools.role: Builds the deviation list, drives HYSYS, stores a snapshot of each state and supports analysis and reporting.

build_steps.step: Connect to an open simulation case and check which streams and units can be deviated.
Let the user choose streams, parameters and deviation ranges, from which the deviation list is generated and then simulated.
After each run, save a snapshot of key process variables for all streams.
Interrogate the snapshots with fixed questions such as loss of reaction, runaway possibility, the most sensitive stream and unexpected vapour.
Sweep the deviation magnitude continuously and look at the rate of change to find step changes.

key_choices.value: Deviations are expressed as percent of design value; feed temperature was swept from +30% to -30% (175 to 325 degC).
Results are evaluated with a human expert team; the tool is support, not replacement.

profiles.tool_chain: Tool generates deviations, HYSYS solves them, snapshots go to a shared database, and the analysis module writes a HAZOP-like table.

validation.detail: No numerical comparison. The authors note that the simulated multiple steady states resemble the behaviour described by Morud and Skogestad (1998).

sensitivity.detail: Deviation-magnitude sweeps found a drop of about 60% in reactor outlet temperature near an 18% feed-temperature deviation, attributed to a shift between steady states.

limitations.text: Uncertainty in any model input can strongly change the results of a model-based HAZOP.
The method is only as complete as the mathematical model is reliable.

profiles.lesson: Sweep each deviation over a wide continuous range and flag discontinuities: a single high or low value can miss a jump to another operating branch.
profiles.caveats: Short conference-style paper; property package, reactor kinetics and solver mode are not stated. No comparison with plant data.

profiles.title: Computer Aided HAZOP Study Implementation Bottlenecks in Chemical Industry
profiles.read_scope: Full paper
profiles.objective: Review where simulation-based HAZOP results can mislead, using an alkylpyridine N-oxidation CSTR and an ammonia synthesis reactor.

tools.name: Aspen HYSYS
tools.role: Ammonia synthesis case.

tools.name: MATLAB
tools.role: Authors' own N-oxidation reactor model.

build_steps.step: Use HAZOP guide words to generate the simulation inputs, then grade the severity of each simulated state.
Give each qualitative deviation a numerical size and duration before it can be simulated.
Extend the deviation range far enough, including the return path, to detect multiple steady states.
Perturb an uncertain model parameter (here the reaction enthalpy) and see whether the map of safe operating points moves.

key_choices.value: Reactor temperature to be held within 110 to 125 degC.
Reaction enthalpy raised by 10%.

validation.detail: This is a retrospective critique of the authors' earlier simulations; no new comparison with measurements is reported.

sensitivity.detail: A 10% higher reaction enthalpy greatly moved the simulated safe operating regions. Below 210 degC fresh-feed temperature the ammonia reactor temperature dropped rapidly.

limitations.text: Simulation-based HAZOP results still need verification and further analysis by experienced engineers.
Too narrow a deviation range can hide potentially severe events.

profiles.lesson: For reactive nodes, propagate model-parameter uncertainty (the paper tested reaction enthalpy) through the deviation study; a safe-region result computed with one parameter set is not a safety conclusion.
profiles.caveats: Short paper; HYSYS version and model details are deferred to earlier publications.

profiles.title: Dispersion modelling for explosion risk analysis
profiles.read_scope: entire paper
profiles.objective: Validate FLACS flammable cloud volumes against offshore-module release experiments and test the frozen-cloud shortcut used in explosion risk analysis.

tools.name: FLACS
tools.version: not stated (v10.1 user manual is cited)
tools.role: CFD dispersion in a naturally ventilated offshore module

build_steps.step: Convert point concentration measurements into flammable volume by assigning each monitor a cell volume, so the validation target matches the explosion-analysis input.
Run a grid sensitivity on one experiment at three cell sizes before choosing the grid.
Pick further cases that span release position and direction, flow rate, wind and module wall layout.
Investigate an outlier by changing wind speed within experimental error, refining the wake mesh and lowering the cloud concentration threshold.
Test frozen-cloud scaling by grouping experiments with the same release and wind direction and predicting each from the others.

key_choices.value: 0.5 m, because 0.25 m was not worth its cost given the small differences.
FLACS k-epsilon; large objects resolved on grid and small ones as sub-grid drag and turbulence sources.
Factor of 1.5 on measured volume, as the experimental report gave no error bars.
Software guidance limits the mix factor to 0.5 to 2.

profiles.tool_chain: FLACS concentrations become flammable cloud volumes, which would feed explosion risk analysis; frozen-cloud scaling by mass rate over ventilation rate substitutes for extra CFD runs.

validation.detail: 1999 joint-industry offshore module releases. The author reports good agreement apart from two cases with jet impingement on a vessel (over-predicted) and C17, under-predicted by about a factor of 4 (about 3 after higher wind and refined wake). Table 2 also shows A02 (240 against 152 m3) and A15 (1656 against 1088 m3) slightly above the paper's factor-1.5 band. For C17, a 4% threshold gave similar measured and computed volumes.

sensitivity.detail: Three grid sizes, wind speed and wake resolution, and flammable-limit threshold.

limitations.text: The validation data used for the frozen-cloud check are limited and grouped wind directions were not truly constant.
Frozen-cloud predictions scatter widely and should be verified with CFD for each parameter group before use.

profiles.lesson: Validate the quantity the risk analysis consumes (cloud volume), report its sensitivity to the concentration threshold, and verify frozen-cloud scaling per release group before relying on it.
profiles.caveats: Short consultancy paper. The conclusions say case C17 was over-predicted although the tables and results text show it under-predicted. Grid study based on a single experiment.

profiles.title: Evaluation of Fire Dynamics Simulator for Liquefied Natural Gas Vapor Dispersion Hazards
profiles.read_scope: abstract, parts of chapter 6 (scientific assessment), chapter 7, start of chapter 8 and the statistical measures table, validation summary, uncertainty analyses, chapter 9; individual trial sections only sampled
profiles.objective: Apply the US LNG vapour dispersion model evaluation protocol (scientific assessment, verification, validation) to FDS and recommend how it should be used for siting studies.

tools.name: Fire Dynamics Simulator (FDS)
tools.role: CFD (large eddy) dispersion model under evaluation

tools.name: ABS/FERC pool spread model
tools.role: Calculated the vapour source term supplied to FDS for spills

build_steps.step: Assess the model's physics against the protocol's qualitative criteria, noting what needs separate sub-models such as flashing, jetting and pool spread.
For verification, review the developer's quality assurance evidence and verification guide rather than auditing code line by line.
Compute each spill's vapour source with a separate pool spread model from flow rate and duration.
Drive field-trial runs with the measured transient upwind wind, and run until a quasi-steady wind field exists before opening the gas source.
Score the protocol's field and wind-tunnel trials, split into unobstructed and obstructed groups and short and long time averages.
Turn the observed underprediction bounds into recommended concentration safety factors for each flow-field class.

key_choices.value: A base grid of 2 x 2 x 1 m was used for the Maplin Sands, Burro, Coyote and Thorney Island field trials and the CHRC tunnel tests; some other series used other base grids.
Transient measured wind was used; the imposed fluctuations decay across the domain, which the author links partly to more far-field overprediction.
The protocol's roughness values are considered generally low, which can make the model look more conservative than it is.
Short averages are recommended for flammable centreline concentration because longer averages smooth peaks.
2 (half LFL) without obstructions and 3 (one third LFL) with obstructions or sloped terrain.

profiles.tool_chain: Spill flow rate and duration feed the ABS/FERC pool spread model; its pool area and vaporisation rate become the FDS gas source; measured weather sets the boundary conditions; FDS outputs are scored with statistical performance measures.

validation.detail: Compared with the protocol's experiments. For unobstructed field trials the author finds good agreement or overprediction of maximum arc-wise concentrations over land and a tendency to underpredict over water. The obstructed Falcon 1 and 3 field trials were underpredicted by about a factor of 2 (Falcon 4 overpredicted). Unobstructed sloped wind-tunnel cases were underpredicted by about a factor of 3, and obstructed scaled wind-tunnel cases agreed worse, mostly underpredicted by a factor of 2 or more.

sensitivity.detail: The uncertainty chapter discusses source term, averaging, grid, wind, roughness, stability, ambient conditions and composition, but a systematic grid refinement is left as a recommendation.

limitations.text: The recommendations depend on the settings used in the study, including grid resolution.
The source term strongly controls the result but is outside what the protocol examines.
Scatter in point-by-point concentrations is wide, with many near-zero predictions away from the plume centreline.

profiles.lesson: A protocol evaluation is only valid for the grid, source model and boundary treatment tested; carry those settings, and the matching safety factor, into the application study or re-validate.
profiles.caveats: Masters thesis; this is not a regulatory approval of FDS. The model version is old. Safety factors are the author's recommendation from this setup.

profiles.title: Risk Assessment of a Hydrogen Refueling Station in an Urban Area
profiles.read_scope: HTML text of method, results, discussion and conclusions; table contents and figures were mostly not rendered
profiles.objective: Judge whether a hydrogen refuelling station in central Seoul is acceptably sited, using HyRAM jet-fire and overpressure results and a French land-use-planning severity and frequency matrix.

tools.name: HyRAM
tools.role: Jet-fire heat flux and overpressure for leak scenarios.

tools.name: PHAST
tools.role: Overpressure impact diameters, including catastrophic rupture, without the mitigation wall.

build_steps.step: Take weather from a national worst-case and alternative-leak-scenario guideline for flammable gases.
Take leak scenario frequencies from a Sandia report for the largest hydrogen inventories.
Compute heat flux at chosen points and compare with the national code safety distance.
Add a catastrophic rupture case in the second tool because the first did not simulate it.
Count exposed people from district population density times effect area, excluding the station footprint, and place each scenario on the severity-frequency matrix.

key_choices.value: 3919 persons per km2 for the district.
French land-use values: 200 mbar (5 percent lethality), 140 mbar (1 percent), 50 mbar (irreversible effects).
Birch et al. formulation among the options offered.
At or below 1e-6 per year taken as typical of general QRAs.

profiles.tool_chain: HyRAM gives jet-fire and overpressure results; PHAST effect diameters plus population density set the severity class, which is paired with a frequency class in the matrix.

validation.detail: No comparison with data; the two tools are not systematically compared.

sensitivity.detail: None reported.

limitations.text: Results do not credit safety measures that would shorten the fatality distances.
The 2D integral and engineering tools may not capture the rise of buoyant hydrogen; CFD is suggested.
Initiators such as vehicle impact, power loss and natural events were not covered.

profiles.lesson: Check that every scenario hole size is physically possible for the pipe bore before taking generic leak frequencies; here the tabulated large leak exceeded the orifice diameter and the tool could not run it.
profiles.caveats: The publisher site refused the fetch, so a Wayback copy was read. Tool version for HyRAM, weather values and several tables are missing from the text. The authors lower the large-leak frequency by argument without quantifying it, and the safety conclusion partly rests on a mitigation wall and on that argument.

profiles.title: Assessment of Uncertainties in Risk Analysis of Chemical Establishments. The ASSURANCE project. Final summary report
profiles.institution_or_venue: Risoe National Laboratory, Risoe-R-1344(EN), with EC Joint Research Centre
profiles.read_scope: uncertainty framing, chapters 3 to 5 (plant, qualitative phase, frequency and consequence comparison), chapters 7 and 8; the land-use planning chapter only in part
profiles.objective: Benchmark exercise in which seven teams independently analysed the same ammonia storage plant, to measure and explain the spread between quantitative risk analyses.

tools.name: Each team's own QRA methods and tools (not named in the parts read)
tools.role: Quantitative risk analysis of the common plant

tools.name: Fault trees, event trees and generic data
tools.role: Frequency assessment, in different combinations between teams

build_steps.step: Give all teams one documented reference plant, with a single site visit, shared question-and-answer material, common assumptions and fictitious data where needed.
Let each team do hazard identification and screening, then compare the selected scenarios and the ranking conventions.
Each team quantifies its own scenarios plus a common set of reference scenarios, so that results can be compared item by item.
Tabulate each team's top-event frequencies and underlying assumptions (pipe length, use factor, components, failure causes, data source) to find causes of deviation.
Rerun the frequencies with agreed site characteristics (pipe length, use factor, number of transfers, tanks in use) to remove deviation caused by ambiguous inputs.
Break consequence modelling into outflow, pool, dispersion and dose-response stages and list the sources of uncertainty at each.

key_choices.value: Imposed where possible in the quantitative phase to remove their influence on the comparison.

key_choices.item: Scenario definition for catastrophic tank rupture
key_choices.value: Left to the teams at first; definitions ranged from instantaneous loss of the whole inventory to partial roof failure, giving different source terms.

key_choices.item: Ammonia evaporation fraction for release onto water
key_choices.value: Teams assumed anywhere from 8% to 60% of the total release evaporated, a main reason this scenario showed the largest consequence discrepancy.
Time-varying release rates had to be reduced to average, maximum, minimum or corrected values by judgement when the dispersion model could not take them.
An analyst judgement; the dispersion models used were all box models with similar structure.

profiles.tool_chain: Hazard identification and screening produce the scenario list; frequency structures and generic data give top-event frequencies; outflow, pool evaporation, dispersion and probit steps give consequences; both are combined into individual and societal risk and then compared for land-use planning.

validation.detail: Team-to-team comparison only. After fixing common site characteristics the authors say the frequency spread was considerably reduced, basically to 1 to 2 orders of magnitude, except for loading-arm scenario 17; their summary table still lists maximum-to-minimum frequency ratios of 615 for loading-arm scenario 4 and 248 for scenario 7*, besides 14000 for scenario 17. The ranking of least probable scenarios agreed among the probabilistic teams, and the largest differences overall were in frequencies.

sensitivity.detail: A case study fixed common site characteristics and recalculated frequencies; the authors also give a qualitative star ranking of factors, with scenario definition ranked highest.

limitations.text: The qualitative ranking of uncertainty factors comes from this exercise and is not claimed to hold for all plants and analyses.
Part of the frequency spread came from limited access to plant staff and an ambiguously worded scenario set, which may be particular to the exercise.
Parameter uncertainty was the only one of the three uncertainty types that could be measured.

profiles.lesson: Before comparing or trusting QRA numbers, fix and publish scenario definitions, pipe lengths, use factors, transfer counts, failure-data source and source-term averaging; much of the spread comes from these choices rather than from the solver.
profiles.caveats: Single facility and one substance (toxic ammonia); the exercise dates from about 2000 and tools have changed. The report masks the plant and uses altered surroundings and fictitious population data. Figures were not readable in the text extraction.

profiles.title: Dynamic simulation of a centrifugal compressor system
profiles.read_scope: introduction, chapter 3 modelling and scenarios, chapter 4 validation, start of chapter 5, conclusions
profiles.objective: Build and check a dynamic model of an offshore two-stage gas compression system and use it to study shutdown, start-up and step changes for a planned modification.

tools.name: Aspen HYSYS Dynamics
tools.role: dynamic compressor, anti-surge and control model

build_steps.step: Enter vendor compressor curves, motor and compressor inertia and driver torque-speed data; extrapolate other speeds when only one speed curve exists.
Specify flows at gas inlets and pressures at outlets so the volume upstream of the compressor behaves realistically.
Replace the software surge-line polynomial with a molecular-weight-independent surge correlation in a spreadsheet where surge varies with gas weight.
Validate the as-built version on gas-sampled steady states and on logged shutdown and start-up transients before changing it to the new design.
Check start-up duration against the plant (6.5 s simulated, 5 to 7 s observed).
In shutdown studies from near the surge line, vary surge margin, anti-surge valve Cv and speed, inertia and discharge volume.

key_choices.value: Peng-Robinson for gas; NRTL for the water/TEG cooling medium.
No wall heat transfer or wall heat storage.
Simple flow-scaled UA; a more detailed model was rejected as slow and giving unreasonable results.

profiles.tool_chain: Vendor datasheets and curves plus gas samples feed the existing-system model; after validation it is rebuilt with the new compressor data for scenario runs.

validation.detail: Gas-sampled steady states showed temperature and some pressure differences, and the authors found it hard to draw conclusions given measurement uncertainty. They conclude that dynamic behaviour for start-up time, flow and pressures was similar to the plant and that start-up time fell within the plant's range. In logged shutdown and start-up, changes in flow, pressure and temperature were faster in the simulation, temperature transients agreed poorly, and in the shutdown the model surged in both stages while the readings showed no sign of first-stage surge.

sensitivity.detail: Surge margin, anti-surge valve size and opening speed, inertia, discharge volume, curve extrapolation and controller tuning.

limitations.text: Temperature predictions are doubtful without wall heat transfer and storage.
Faster model dynamics can overstate the tendency to surge.
The software handles surge poorly and its default low-speed curve extrapolation tends to overestimate head.
Plant logs resolved no faster than one reading per second.

profiles.lesson: Validate compressor trips against logged transients, not only steady points, and review pipe volumes, wall thermal mass, sensor response and off-curve extrapolation before sizing anti-surge hardware from the model.
profiles.caveats: Master's thesis; control tunings were not the plant's; dynamic datasets lacked gas composition and some inlet flows, so comparison is mainly qualitative.

profiles.title: Diseño de seguridad inherente
profiles.read_scope: Parts of chapter 4 (index sub-scores), chapter 5 acetone and cumene cases and comparison, chapter 6 conclusions
profiles.objective: Score alternative or example process routes with the Heikkila Inherent Safety Index, including a conventional versus reactive-distillation cumene comparison.

tools.name: Aspen Plus
tools.role: Estimated reaction heats where the literature flowsheet did not report them.

build_steps.step: Take flows, temperatures, pressures and conversions from published flowsheets, and use the simulator to fill in missing reaction heats from operating conditions and conversions.
Normalise reaction heat by the mass entering the reactor over a nominal one hour, then map it to the sub-index band.
Estimate inventory from the inlet flows of the main units inside battery limits over one hour, excluding off-battery streams.
Set flammability, explosivity and toxicity sub-scores from the worst compound using public chemical database properties.
Sum the sub-indices and compare routes line by line to see which sub-scores drive the difference.

key_choices.value: Heikkila Inherent Safety Index; the cumene reactive-distillation route scored lower (safer) than the conventional route by 4 points.
For reactive distillation the reactive section of the column is scored as the reactor for equipment safety.

profiles.tool_chain: Literature flowsheet data feed Aspen Plus reaction-heat estimates, which feed manual index scoring.

sensitivity.detail: No sensitivity of scores to inventory basis or judgement-based sub-indices was found in the sections read.

limitations.text: The sub-indices and the way of determining them are not absolute and may miss parameters of a particular process.
The author sees equipment and process-structure sub-indices as the most problematic because they rest on accident statistics.

profiles.lesson: State the inventory basis explicitly. An hour of inlet flow is not equipment hold-up, and in intensified designs such as reactive distillation that choice can decide whether the minimisation benefit appears at all.
profiles.caveats: Bachelor thesis in Spanish; the simulator has a minor role. The structure sub-index is set to 0 (recommended) even where the text notes serious fire hazards. Read from a web archive copy.

Concrete floor and ceiling and solid brick walls, with thermal properties listed in the text.
ISO 9705 room (2.4 m wide, 3.6 m long, 2.4 m high) with a single vent opening.
20 degrees C and 101 kPa.

Rebuild the HYSYS model in the second simulator and tune the reflux ratio until the steady state is close to the original.
Convert to dynamic mode after adding tray dimensions, then check that the dynamic base case matches the steady state.
Apply the deviation after 5 hours of simulated normal operation.
When automatically inserted controllers hide a deviation, weaken or neutralise them and repeat the run to expose the uncontrolled response.

key_choices.value: A different simulator from the company's was used because only it was available at the university with dynamics.
The solver would not converge with a fully closed valve, so it was left 2% open.
The ratio could only be changed in the steady-state model, so a series of steady-state cases was exported to dynamics one by one.

profiles.lesson: Before using a pressure-driven or flow-driven dynamic model for HAZOP, check what the boundary specifications and auto-inserted controllers hold constant: a fixed pressure can reverse or erase the consequence you are looking for.
profiles.caveats: Master's thesis; text is in Portuguese. The external-fire case was imitated by raising ambient temperature with software default heat-transfer values and is not a fire load model. Steady state, isothermal gasification, char as solid carbon, no tar.

tools.role: Explosion overpressure of gas clouds in the enclosure

tools.name: ANSYS Fluent

Swap to hydrogen and blends with the same geometry, congestion and cloud sizes, then find the cloud size that keeps the original overpressure limit.
Run ventilation alone to locate low-velocity zones and choose worst-case leak positions and directions.
Represent the leak as mass, momentum and energy sources in a small volume, with momentum from choked flow.
Repeat identical leak cases for hydrogen, changing gas properties, flammable limit and allowable cloud volume, and compare concentrations at the outlet detector plane.

k-epsilon, stated to follow the HSE joint-industry CFD best-practice guidance.
The methane limit of 0.1% of enclosure volume was rejected for hydrogen.
Six worst-case positions and directions.

sensitivity.detail: Fuel blends and cloud sizes were varied, but no grid or model sensitivity is reported.

limitations.text: The limiting cloud size may not transfer to other enclosures because volume and congestion effects were not studied.

profiles.lesson: Changing fuel changes the acceptance cloud size as well as the dispersion, so derive the criterion first and then re-run the ventilation study.
profiles.caveats: The paper gives no mesh details, grid study or code versions, and shows pressure results only in normalised form. Hydrogen explosion predictions are not validated against hydrogen data in this paper.

build_steps.step: Pick the sizing scenario after hazard identification; here loss of reactor cooling.
Define reaction stoichiometry, rate and heats of formation from calorimetry, then check the model against that same calorimeter run.
Code the missing two-phase safety-valve flow model (ISO omega method) in Custom Modeler and couple it as a subroutine.
Repeat runs over vent sizes to find the size that prevents the pressure rise, for a closed reactor and one with an exhaust line.
Test at small scale with valve diameters chosen by keeping the ratio of vent area to liquid volume constant.

Safety valve on the reactor top with an assumed set pressure of 400 kPag; results also compared with and without an exhaust gas line.

profiles.tool_chain: ARSST data give the reaction model; Aspen property data and Aspen Dynamics solve the reactor; the Custom Modeler valve routine returns vent flow; predicted vent sizes are scaled to the 40 mL test.

validation.detail: Small-scale tests agreed well with the model without an exhaust line; with an exhaust line the measurements differed from the calculation.

The smaller computed vent sizes include no safety allowance.
With the exhaust line, experiment and simulation did not correspond because pressure rose faster than a safety valve can handle.
In one exhaust-line case predicted to be adequately relieved, pressure rose to about 1,000 kPag.

profiles.lesson: When dynamic simulation reduces a required vent size, check valve opening time and pressure-rise rate and test the unfavourable configuration; removing volatile solvent early can make the later runaway worse.
profiles.caveats: Short paper; kinetics, property method and numerical results of the comparison plots are not tabulated. The text itself reports pressure-rise rate far above the cited ISO limit for valve relief, so the reduced vent size is not demonstrated for that case. Not a design basis.

tools.name: ALOHA

Check whether simplifying to methane or three components hides liquid or aerosol phases at release conditions.
Screen release and weather parameters with integral tools.
In CFD, first establish the wind profile in a steady run and use it to initialise the transient release run.
Validate against the Prairie Grass field trial with grid and turbulence-treatment sensitivity, using factor-of-two criteria.

About 2 million cells chosen after four grids; the two finest were treated as equivalent.
Synthetic eddy inflow cost far more run time without significantly different estimates.
The author finds toxic distances very sensitive above about 15 mol% hydrogen sulphide, where multicomponent thermodynamics should be used.

profiles.tool_chain: HYSYS phase behaviour guides the model class and composition sets; ALOHA and Canary screen source and weather parameters; OpenFOAM with a steady-state wind field then simulates selected compositions.

validation.detail: CFD against one Prairie Grass field trial run: the author reports comparable values on one side of the centreline, overprediction near the centreline and underprediction farther from it, and says performance statistics were satisfactory at the 400 m and 800 m arcs.

The CFD runs represented natural gas by only methane and hydrogen sulphide.
Different tools can give substantially different distances for one accident, apparently more so for liquid or two-phase storage.

profiles.lesson: Check the phase envelope of the real composition before simplifying it, and record the equation of state and expansion method as sensitivity inputs to the dispersion study.
profiles.caveats: The literature review says Peng-Robinson or Soave-Redlich-Kwong should not be used when the H2S fraction exceeds a few percent; chapters 4 and 7 report using Peng-Robinson in HYSYS for compositions up to 29% H2S, and no reconciliation was found in the parts read. profiles.title: Nuclear Power Plant Fire Modeling Analysis Guidelines (NPP FIRE MAG), NUREG-1934 / EPRI 1023259, Final Report

profiles.objective: Give a staged process for applying fire models, including FDS, in nuclear plant fire hazard analysis, with validation applicability, grid and uncertainty treatment.

tools.name: FDS
tools.role: CFD fire model among five covered model tools

build_steps.step: Define goals, characterise scenarios, select models, compute, analyse sensitivity and uncertainty, then document.
Compute the characteristic fire diameter and set trial cell sizes by its ratio to cell size, then refine until differences are small relative to expected model accuracy.
Check geometry files made by pre-processors against what was intended.
Compare scenario non-dimensional parameters with the validation experiments' ranges.
If outside range, vary inputs conservatively into range and see whether the conclusion changes; justify anything else separately.
Apply tabulated model bias and scatter to estimate the probability that a damage threshold is exceeded.

key_choices.value: Characteristic diameter over cell size of 5 to 10 usually favourable for gross smoke movement.
At least three across any flow path and the fire.
Heat release rate is almost always among the controlling parameters.
Use power-law dependence, for example hot-layer temperature rise with heat release to the two-thirds power.

profiles.tool_chain: Scenario definition leads to model choice and applicability check, then computation, then bias and scatter adjustment and sensitivity before documentation.

validation.detail: The guide summarises bias and scatter derived from the separate NUREG-1824 verification and validation study.

sensitivity.detail: Method guidance: grid series and input sensitivity are prescribed rather than a single study reported.

limitations.text: The validation experiments were chosen for nuclear plant spaces, so many applications fall outside their range.
Measurement uncertainty that is overestimated leads to underestimated model error.

profiles.lesson: Make grid acceptance relative to known model error, and keep an explicit applicability table with a rule for every parameter that falls outside it.
profiles.caveats: Written for nuclear power plant applications; the FDS manuals cited are for version 5 and the bias and scatter statistics come from NUREG-1824. The guide expects that study to be updated from time to time and notes that new model releases occur, so check for current validation statistics. Applicability outside nuclear plants is not addressed in the sections read.

profiles.title: Verification and Validation of Selected Fire Models for Nuclear Power Plant Applications, Supplement 1 (Draft Report for Comment), NUREG-1824 Supplement 1 / EPRI 3002002182
authors: U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, Office of Nuclear Regulatory Research
profiles.institution_or_venue: US NRC and EPRI (regulator and industry research report)

profiles.objective: Quantify the predictive capability of five fire models against experiments representative of nuclear plant fires, as bias and scatter that analysts can apply to predictions.

tools.name: Fire Dynamics Tools (FDTs)
tools.role: Empirical correlation library under validation

tools.name: CFAST
tools.role: Zone model under validation

tools.name: MAGIC
tools.role: Zone model under validation

tools.name: FDS
tools.role: CFD model under validation

tools.name: FIVE
tools.role: Empirical correlation library under validation

build_steps.step: Define the application's typical fire scenarios and the predicted quantities that matter to them.
Select experiments with public, well-documented data and a well-characterised heat release rate.
Express each experiment and plant scenario with normalised parameters to check whether an application lies inside the validated range.
Estimate experimental uncertainty by combining measurement uncertainty with the effect of input uncertainty propagated through simple models.
For each model and output quantity compute a bias factor and a relative standard deviation that accounts for experimental uncertainty.
Apply them to a prediction: correct for bias, then compute the probability that the true value exceeds a damage threshold.

key_choices.value: Follows ASTM E1355 for evaluating deterministic fire models.
Quantitative uncertainty table replaces the earlier qualitative colour chart.
Where reports gave none, it was estimated from the few that did, plus engineering judgement.
Metrics apply only to the listed model versions, not earlier ones.

validation.detail: FDS was generally the most accurate, then zone models, then correlations, with exceptions. Zone and CFD models all overpredicted smoke concentration by roughly a factor of three.

sensitivity.detail: Input uncertainties were propagated through simple models to estimate experimental uncertainty; this is not a sensitivity study of an application.

limitations.text: Verification of the models is not addressed directly; references are given instead.
Not all plant scenarios are covered and experimental data are limited, so users must judge applicability.
The analyst remains responsible for justifying the model for each application.

profiles.lesson: Publish model accuracy as bias and scatter per output quantity, with the validated range in dimensionless terms, so a prediction can be turned into a probability of exceeding a limit.
profiles.caveats: This is the draft for public comment (the text carries a November 2014 date); any later version was not read, so numbers may differ. The executive summary says verification is not addressed directly, while the conclusions say the five models have been verified by the study as appropriate for fire-protection applications within their assumptions. Read from a Web Archive copy. Fire in compartments for nuclear plants, not process-plant jet or pool fires.

profiles.title: Selected process safety systems analysed using dynamic simulations: A study of the Flare and the High Integrity Pressure Protection Systems
profiles.read_scope: Methodology chapters 4-5, results and discussion chapters 6-7, conclusions, part of the appended draft paper

tools.name: Aspen HYSYS Dynamics
tools.role: Dynamic emergency depressurisation of three flare networks and blockage-driven pressure build-up for HIPPS timing.

tools.name: Aspen HYSYS Event Scheduler
tools.role: Triggers the downstream blockage at a set simulation time.

tools.name: Aspen Flare System Analyzer (existing models)
tools.role: Source of flare piping and fittings data and the steady-state reference.

build_steps.step: Build the HYSYS flare network from existing flare analyser data and first run it with fixed source pressures to compare against that reference before going dynamic.
For the dynamic depressurisation case, open every blowdown valve at once and switch boundaries to zero-flow sources with a pressure boundary at the flare.
Add a third, more detailed flare case that includes dead legs and inactive relief and control valve tail pipes, to test how much hold-up volume matters.
For HIPPS, model the blockage as a normally fully open valve that closes, with the ESD valves assumed to fail, so pressure builds upstream.
Compute PST from the pressure trace as the time between reaching the HIPPS set point and reaching the maximum allowable working pressure.
Compare several pipe pressure-drop correlations for their effect on the HIPPS time response.

key_choices.value: Peng-Robinson; C7+ fractions as lumped hypothetical components.

key_choices.item: Flare run length and time step
key_choices.value: 15 min simulated at a 0.01 s step; the 15 min follows the API 521 depressuring recommendation as quoted by the author.
ESD alarm 140 bar, HIPPS alarm 155 bar, design pressure (MAWP) 170 bar.
Well inlets are fixed-flow sources so inflow stays constant during the blockage; the outlet is a pressure boundary.
Beggs and Brill (1973 and 1979), HTFS homogeneous, Tulsa Unified and a simplified friction model compared; the author prefers Tulsa as it generally gives the shortest PST.
Flare piping split into many segments or increments to offset the weakness of the pipe pressure-drop method for compressible gas.

profiles.tool_chain: Flare analyser piping data and steady-state plant simulation compositions feed the HYSYS dynamic flare models; the HIPPS study is a separate HYSYS flowsheet whose pressure traces give PST.

validation.detail: A fixed-pressure HYSYS run was set up to be checked against the existing flare analyser model (peak load, relief rates, pipe pressure drops); the sections read report no numerical agreement for that check. No plant or test data for HIPPS PST.

sensitivity.detail: Pipe correlation, feed rate, blockage location and elevation ratio were varied; the quoted conclusion is that the simplified friction model gave unreliable, longer (less conservative) PST.

limitations.text: The HYSYS pipe segment cannot represent phase slip; the author judges this negligible for the mostly vapour flare lines studied.
Irregularities in the Tulsa-model pressure curves are attributed to possible numerical instability in the software, not physics.
The finding that elevation detail matters little is not conclusive: elevation ratios were varied on only one 100 m segment.

profiles.lesson: When a simulator supplies PST for a fast safeguard such as a HIPPS, treat the pipe pressure-drop correlation and boundary specification as sensitivity cases and report the shortest credible time. The tabulated values ranged from about 1.5 s to about 211 s; the largest comes from the simplified friction model, which the author considers unreliable (the four flow correlations reach 164 s).
profiles.caveats: The HIPPS layout is hypothetical. Section 7.1 labels Case 1 as Beggs and Brill (1979), although Case 1 is defined as the 1973 version. With the Tulsa model, PST rises between 180,000 and 200,000 kg/h in scenarios 2 and 4; the author flags this and suggests numerical instability. Section 7.1 links the longer PST of the 1979 Beggs and Brill case to over-estimated pressure drop, while the conclusions link the longer PST of the simplified model to under-estimated pressure drop.

tools.role: Integral-model comparison

tools.name: HYSYS
tools.role: Release rate, temperature and composition at the vent, including heavy-component condensation

build_steps.step: Select time windows of the field campaign where release and weather are stable and extract release, wind and gas data.
Compute the vent source term with a process simulator and take inflow conditions from measured meteorology.
Start from each developer's recommended numerical set-up.
Compare plume path with infrared and camera images and concentration decay with sensors, case by case.
After the base comparison, vary ground roughness, source meshing, turbulence constants and wind speed.

key_choices.value: Area leak resolved by 12 cells (at least 4), not a point leak; leak cell surface must equal the real source area.
5% intensity and length scale 15% of vent diameter.
Developer guidance: at most 1 m cells at domain boundaries and stretch ratios below 1.1.
Adaptive on concentration gradients, from 5 mm near the vent to 1 m far away.
0.9, which gave longer distances than 0.7 and closer agreement.
No higher than 5 mm recommended.

profiles.tool_chain: HYSYS defines the vent stream; that source and measured meteorology drive FLACS, CFX and Phast; concentration decay and plume path are compared.

validation.detail: ENGIE Montoir LNG vapour vent tests. 6-inch horizontal: LFL distance errors of -1% (FLACS) and +20% (CFX), Phast 23% short. 6-inch vertical: FLACS and CFX distances judged pertinent, CFX conservative at about +41%, Phast strongly under-predicting near-field concentration. 18-inch vertical: FLACS and CFX under-predicted LFL distance by around 47% and 31%, Phast by around 18%.

sensitivity.detail: Roughness, FLACS leak meshing, CFX turbulence constants and wind speed. A point leak shortened distances by 27% to 39% against a 12-cell area leak.

limitations.text: Even the best code can be non-conservative for low-momentum cold heavy releases, especially at low concentrations.
Predicting 20% LFL distances with confidence in any atmospheric condition was judged very unlikely.

profiles.lesson: For elevated cold jets, treat the leak mesh, roughness and wind speed as part of the source definition and test them; a dedicated safety CFD code is not automatically conservative.
profiles.caveats: Short paper showing only part of the results; mesh sizes for the actual runs and code versions are not given. The 18-inch FLACS error is quoted as about -47% in one place and -48% in another.

tools.name: PHAST

tools.name: RiskCurves
tools.role: Individual risk contours.

build_steps.step: Run a preliminary hazard analysis, then carry only representative scenarios from the two highest severity classes, as initiating events, into simulation.
Model pipe ruptures with the PHAST line-rupture model and the storage tank with the catastrophic-rupture model.
Update a diffuse lognormal prior with several generic failure databases (population-variability stage only, since no plant data exist).
Build event trees with immediate and delayed ignition branches and multiply them by the initiating frequency.
Combine frequencies and consequences in a risk tool and identify which initiating event sets the contour.

key_choices.value: Treated as pure methane.
2 minutes assuming automatic isolation, following the Purple Book.
30 seconds, because nearby workers can start the emergency system.
Directly on water with no bund, chosen as conservative because dike areas could not be estimated.
Day and night averages from three years (2006-2008) of MM5 mesoscale simulation taken from a nearby refinery environmental study.
0.2, as very few ignition sources offshore (Cox, Lees and Ang).
Excluded because the offshore cloud has no confinement.
Frequencies kept in the event trees but jet fire left out of the risk because its ranges were negligible beside flash and pool fire.

profiles.tool_chain: PHAST consequence distances plus event-tree frequencies (initiating frequencies from the Bayesian step) are combined in RiskCurves.

validation.detail: No comparison with experiment or another consequence tool for this study.

sensitivity.detail: Not a parametric study; the risk contours are recomputed without the dominant initiating event to show its influence.

limitations.text: The dominant loading-arm frequency rests on opinions from only two experts and is therefore quite uncertain.
With no plant-specific data only the first Bayesian stage was applied, so frequencies rest on generic data.

profiles.lesson: Rank initiating events by their contribution to the risk contour, not by consequence reach: here the largest-range event was not the one that set the intolerable contour. Spend frequency effort on the one that does.
profiles.caveats: Master's thesis. Section 6.2.4 places gas-release event EI03 above 100 kg/s and EI04 between 10 and 100 kg/s, and assigns them immediate-ignition probabilities of 0.04 and 0.09; the thesis's Table 3.4 gives 0.09 for the higher band and 0.04 for the middle band for a low-reactivity gas. Figure 6.17 is captioned EI06 but the heading inside the tree reads EI05 (with the EI06 frequency). The author notes that the terminal offshore distance was set from the consequence results and that a new distance could be set from the risk results; the finding that the shore is unaffected should be read with that choice in mind.

profiles.title: Modelling advanced reforming of bio-compounds for hydrogen production
profiles.read_scope: abstract, sections 3.2-3.4, 5.2.5, 6.3-6.4, 7.3.5, parts of chapter 8; literature review and cost chapters only in part
profiles.objective: Assess sorption-enhanced chemical looping reforming of bio-oil with equilibrium flowsheets and economics, then study the reduction-calcination step with a dynamic packed-bed model and acetic acid kinetics.

tools.name: Aspen Plus
tools.role: Equilibrium flowsheets giving heat and material balances for thermodynamic and techno-economic work.

tools.name: gPROMS ModelBuilder
tools.role: Dynamic distributed reactor model and kinetic parameter estimation.

build_steps.step: Represent bio-oil first by single model compounds and then by a surrogate mixture matched to elemental composition and thermogravimetric curve.
Model reformers as Gibbs-minimisation reactors for the feasibility stage, stated as a simplifying assumption.
Emulate a cyclic fixed bed in steady state with a series of reactor blocks, passing the solid bed state from one stage to the next.
Replace separation systems that are outside the study aim with recovery-specified separator blocks and literature energy use.
Build the dynamic reactor model hierarchically: validate each sub-process separately, then combine.
Test the fitted kinetic model on extra experiments not used in fitting.

key_choices.value: Peng-Robinson, citing simulator guidance for hydrogen-rich high temperature and pressure service and similar literature models.
Adiabatic Gibbs blocks for the looping stages; adiabatic specified-reaction equilibrium reactor for water-gas shift.
Split-fraction separator with 90% H2 recovery.
Backward finite differences along the axis; 50 to 1000 intervals tested with minimal effect; DASOLV integrator.

profiles.tool_chain: Aspen Plus equilibrium balances feed the cost model and give the off-gas composition used as feed to the gPROMS reduction-calcination model; measured kinetics fitted in gPROMS feed later reactor comparisons.

validation.detail: Reduction and sorption-enhanced reforming sub-models compared graphically with literature experiments (authors report excellent agreement). Fitted kinetic model outlet concentrations: average absolute deviation 10.64%, with 4.34% for H2 and 18.46% for CO. Against an Aspen Plus equilibrium reactor, the authors report a good estimate from 600 to 700 degrees C and divergence outside that range.

sensitivity.detail: Reduction-calcination model varied feed gas, temperature, pressure, flux and sorbent capacity; mesh interval count also checked.

limitations.text: The steady-state flowsheet cannot describe the dynamics of the cyclic process and is only for preliminary economics.
The combined reduction-calcination model still needs experimental validation over a range of conditions.
A full dynamic cycle model is blocked by lack of bio-oil kinetics.

The fitted power-law kinetic model is not readily extrapolated outside the experimental pressure range and needs caution at low temperature or high pressure, where methane formation (not modelled) is likely.

profiles.lesson: Validating sub-models separately does not validate their combination; say so explicitly and keep the claim for the combined model at the feasibility level.
profiles.caveats: The abstract places the dynamic reactor model in Chapter 7, while the body presents it in Chapter 6. Aspen Plus version not stated.

profiles.title: Blowdown of Onshore and Offshore Installations
profiles.institution_or_venue: IChemE Symposium Series No 139 (Imperial College London)
profiles.read_scope: whole paper text; the comparison plots were not examined
profiles.objective: Present the BLOWDOWN program and its validation against small-scale tests and full-installation blowdown measurements, with design lessons on minimum temperatures.

tools.name: BLOWDOWN
tools.role: simulates fluid and wall temperatures, efflux rate, composition and phase during depressurisation

build_steps.step: Split each vessel into gas, liquid hydrocarbon and free-water zones, and divide pipelines into axial elements of adaptive size.
March in discrete pressure steps rather than time steps.
Apply zone-specific wall heat transfer (convection, boiling) with transient conduction through the wall and insulation to the surroundings.
Include connected piping and liquid drainage to low points; in the gas plant case, allowing liquid collection lowered the predicted minimum wall temperature by over 30 K.

key_choices.value: Rigorous properties from an extended corresponding-states method, because errors here distort the whole phase path.
Quasi-steady, homogeneous two-phase flow in topsides pipework (relaxed for pipelines).
The authors state there are no adjustable parameters.

validation.detail: Small-scale vessel and pipeline tests: bulk fluid and wall temperature discrepancy stated as 3 K. Full-installation comparisons (offshore platform, onshore gas plant) are described as generally adequate with somewhat wider stated bands, and with poor agreement at a few locations (see limitations).

sensitivity.detail: Case study on one platform: blowing down a single train rather than all of them lowers minimum wall temperature by about 20 K through lower back-pressure.

limitations.text: Outside wall temperatures on two flare laterals downstream of one blowdown valve agreed badly; the authors attribute this to possible very cold supersonic flow after a choked expansion.
Local steep temperature gradients near tees, bends and expansions are not captured.
Slow sensor response limits comparison on short time scales.

profiles.lesson: Do not assume full-plant simultaneous blowdown is the coldest case for flare piping: run partial blowdowns, include liquid low points and connected upstream/downstream units, and check sensor placement before judging model error.
profiles.caveats: Authored by the code developers; comparisons are mostly graphical and qualitative apart from the quoted bands; older work and a proprietary code; text is a scan-to-text conversion.

profiles.title: Modelling of an industrial plant for vinyl chloride production
profiles.institution_or_venue: Universita degli Studi di Padova, Dipartimento di Ingegneria Industriale
profiles.read_scope: abstract, thermodynamic package and validation (section 3.2 and chapter 4), start of reactor modelling, HCl column results and thermodynamic checks in chapter 6, conclusions
profiles.objective: Build a whole-plant vinyl chloride flowsheet and establish how far its thermodynamic model and results can be trusted by regression on binary data and comparison with literature plant data.

tools.name: gPROMS ProcessBuilder
tools.role: Flowsheet simulation

tools.name: Multiflash (Infochem)
tools.role: Property package with DIPPR pure-component data, also used from Excel for regression

build_steps.step: Choose the thermodynamic model family from component non-ideality and operating pressure.
Identify which binary pairs control the key separations and gas solubilities, and gather data near operating conditions.
Regress interaction parameters by least squares on temperature or pressure with the same property engine the flowsheet uses.
Check dataset consistency from the pattern and size of residuals.
Check pure-component vapour pressures against data, because binary parameters cannot correct errors in them.
Test the effect of parameter sets and an alternative equation of state on the sensitive column against a reference temperature profile and spot flashes.

key_choices.value: NRTL for the liquid with Redlich-Kwong for the vapour, as the pressure limit of an ideal vapour was judged too low.
Fixed at the default 0.3 for all binaries.
Adjusted until direct chlorination selectivity reached 99%.
The vinyl chloride and HCl parameters were left out of the final flowsheet because the results were closer to practice without them.

profiles.tool_chain: Literature binary data are regressed through the Excel interface to the property engine; the resulting property file is imported by the process simulator, whose column results are checked against a reference temperature profile and direct property-engine flashes.

validation.detail: Binary data were fitted and plant-section results compared with literature values; several parts were close to expected values, but HCl and vinyl chloride equilibria with EDC were not reliable. With the full parameter set no vapour was predicted at one HCl column stage condition.

sensitivity.detail: Full versus reduced parameter sets and SRK on the HCl column; reactor design and kinetic parameter sensitivities. Direct chlorination was not affected by the binary parameters.

limitations.text: The HCl column works above HCl's critical temperature, so the Antoine vapour pressure is used outside its validity.
Simulation results are only partly accurate because of the thermodynamic representation.
More data are needed for systems with HCl above its critical temperature.

profiles.lesson: Good binary fits do not validate a flowsheet: check supercritical components and pure vapour pressures, and test the sensitive column with parameter sets switched on and off against an independent profile.
profiles.caveats: Masters thesis with software-vendor support. The comparison data are from literature. A kinetic factor was tuned to a target selectivity, so that selectivity is not validation. Chapter 4 presents NRTL as an activity coefficient model, while the conclusions refer to an NRTL equation of state. Safety use is not the topic; it is a process simulation verification example.

profiles.title: Integrated process and control modelling of water recirculation in once-through boilers during low load and transient operation
profiles.read_scope: abstract, scope and assumptions, sections 3.6-3.7 model, chapter 4 validation, chapter 6 plant implementation, chapter 7
profiles.objective: Model the start-up recirculation loop of a large once-through boiler with its controls, validate it on plant data, and design a better control strategy.

tools.name: Flownex
tools.role: integrated thermo-fluid and control simulation

build_steps.step: Lump parallel tubes into representative pipes and apportion furnace heat to them as scaled fractions of fuel input.
Represent steam outlet pressure and pump and feedwater flows as boundary conditions, and the separators with a two-phase tank element.
Solve the steady state with an external routine that adjusts recirculation flow to close the tank energy balance, then release the boundary and start the transient.
Compare steady states at several loads with averaged control-system readings.
Drive a six-hour cold start with recorded pressure, load and feedwater temperature and compare unforced outputs such as inlet temperature, steam flow and vessel level.

key_choices.value: Homogeneous two-phase flow; main steam valve as a pressure boundary.
Time step 0.1 s with integration weighting factor 0.7.
Boiler efficiency function raised to 103% to correct under-predicted evaporator heat during start-up.

profiles.tool_chain: Plant control-system records are imported by script as time-varying boundary inputs; the validated model is then used to test control changes, later implemented on a unit in commissioning.

validation.detail: Steady states at three loads compared with plant control-system data: generally good, with the largest errors in economiser temperatures and pressure drops, attributed to circulation-flow changes. In a six-hour cold start, compared graphically, the author judges economiser inlet temperature sufficiently accurate and finds main steam flow in good agreement except at very low loads and suspected mill-purge events; collecting-vessel level was also compared.

sensitivity.detail: Single-parameter transient changes (pressure, circulation flow, feedwater temperature, load) with controls off, then with controls on.

limitations.text: Measured fuel input is uncertain, for example unmetered heat from mill purging.
Furnace heat split was scaled linearly from full load and could be improved.
Superheater and downstream pressure control are omitted behind a fixed-pressure boundary.

profiles.lesson: Replaying recorded boundary data through a start-up model is a practical transient check, but report which inputs and calibration factors were imposed or tuned so the remaining outputs can be judged fairly.
profiles.caveats: Master's thesis with an industry sponsor; calibration factor above 100 percent absorbs modelling error; some steady-state calibration also adjusted boundary values and circulation flow; software version not found in the parts read.

profiles.title: Quantitative HAZOP-LOPA analysis of a dimethyl ether distillation unit based on aspen plus steady-state and dynamic simulation
profiles.institution_or_venue: Journal of Physics: Conference Series, vol. 3345 (AMCE-2026)
profiles.read_scope: Full paper
profiles.objective: Quantify a HAZOP of a dimethyl ether column with LOPA frequencies, steady-state safe windows and dynamic operator response times.

tools.name: Aspen Plus
tools.role: Steady-state flowsheet and feed deviation sensitivity.

tools.name: Aspen Plus Dynamics
tools.role: Control-failure transients and response times.

build_steps.step: Run a guide-word HAZOP on the column nodes and treat consequences as LOPA scenarios and causes as initiating events.
Sweep feed flow and feed temperature and tabulate the deviation at which each monitored variable reaches its threshold.
Turn on tray hydraulics so the percentage of flooding load becomes a deviation limit.
Export to dynamics, add control loops, settle for an hour and check recovery from small step disturbances.
For each control failure, take the time to reach a design safety threshold as the available operator response time.

key_choices.value: NRTL.
About 0.01 for a SIL 1 interlock or a relief valve (and about 0.1 for alarm plus operator), referred to CCPS and IEC 61511.
A value of 0.1 per year for a valve failing open was compared with an OREDA-2015 fail-to-open-on-demand rate of the same order.
17.0 bar top pressure, about 60% above normal operating pressure.

profiles.tool_chain: HAZOP deviations feed LOPA arithmetic; the Aspen Plus model gives steady-state thresholds and is exported to Dynamics for response times, which then guide alarm versus SIF allocation.

validation.detail: A section headed model validation says tray composition trends are consistent with distillation theory and compares base-case outputs with design or operating values. The T1 top and bottom pressures and the 80% reactor conversion among them are also given as model design parameters or block specifications. No measured plant or experimental data are described.

sensitivity.detail: Feed flow and temperature swept from -50% to +50%; dynamic cases gave response times from a few minutes (complete condenser failure) to several hours.

limitations.text: Only one compound-fault combination was examined.

profiles.lesson: Use dynamic response times to decide which LOPA operator credits are plausible, but check first that the validation is independent of the inputs and that every number agrees across text, tables and conclusions.
profiles.caveats: Section 4.3 gives the overall safe window for feed flow as -30% to +11% (flooding load), while the abstract and the end of section 4.4 use -30% to +40%; Table 5 places the 80% flooding threshold at +11%. For complete condenser failure section 5 says the top temperature reaches 120 degrees C at about 20 min and that the response time is about 4-5 min, without stating from when the latter is counted. The 0.1 per year frequency for a control valve failing open is supported by comparison with an OREDA-2015 rate for a differently named mode, fail to open on demand. Interlock and relief-valve PFDs are generic order-of-magnitude values, and the 17 bar dynamic limit is not tied to a stated vessel design pressure.

profiles.title: Estudo sobre a modelagem da dispersao atmosferica de gases densos decorrente de liberacoes acidentais em analise quantitativa de risco
profiles.institution_or_venue: Escola Politecnica, Universidade de Sao Paulo
profiles.read_scope: Portuguese original: abstract, chapters 3 to 5 (method, results, conclusions); literature review not read
profiles.objective: Test how the choice of dense gas dispersion model, as embedded in common risk software, changes ammonia hazard distances and individual risk.

tools.name: Phast (UDM)
tools.role: Integral dense gas dispersion

tools.name: Effects (SLAB)
tools.role: Dense gas dispersion with the SLAB model

tools.name: ALOHA (DEGADIS-based and Gaussian)
tools.role: Dense gas and passive plume runs

build_steps.step: Define two release cases from a pressurised ammonia tank: whole inventory over 10 minutes, and a 10 mm hole in the bottom.
Hold source term, weather and topography as uniform as possible across the tools.
Compare downwind distances to concentrations representing 1% and 50% fatality.
Add a Gaussian plume run to show what ignoring dense gas behaviour does.
Combine the distances with assigned scenario frequencies into individual risk against distance for each tool.

key_choices.value: Wind 3.0 m/s at 10 m, stability class C, relative humidity 80%, plus stated air and ground temperatures, taken from the state agency (CETESB) guidance.
0.30 m, as flat open terrain.
1.0E-05 per year for the 10 mm hole and 5.0E-07 per year for the 10-minute inventory release (RIVM).
Only Phast let the user set the transition criterion; its default is a density difference of 0.0015.

profiles.tool_chain: A common release definition feeds each risk package's dispersion model; the distances to the two lethality levels, with fixed frequencies, give individual risk against distance.

validation.detail: No experimental comparison of its own. Distances from the dense gas models stayed within a factor of 2, which the author relates to published performance; the largest differences were between Phast UDM and Effects SLAB, and individual risk curves differed, mostly farther from the source.

sensitivity.detail: Two release sizes and two concentration levels; the text cites a separate paper by the author for a different roughness. No systematic input sensitivity in the thesis chapters read.

limitations.text: Results hold only for the scenarios and conditions used and cannot be generalised to other conditions or substances.

profiles.lesson: Even with matched inputs, the dispersion package can change the individual risk curve; name the package and version in the risk result and check decision distances with a second model.
profiles.caveats: Masters thesis, two release scenarios, one substance, older tool versions, and no comparison of its own with measurements. The mean distances in Tables 19 and 20 equal the average of the three dense gas results, without the Gaussian plume. One sentence in section 4.3 labels the 22% and 29% deviations as scenario 1 and scenario 2, whereas Table 20 shows both are the scenario 2 Phast deviations at the two concentration levels.

profiles.title: Operator Training Simulator for Ethylene Plant
profiles.institution_or_venue: Chemical Engineering Transactions 56 (Universiti Teknologi Malaysia; Petronas Chemical Olefins)
profiles.read_scope: whole paper
profiles.objective: Describe how an operator training simulator for an ethylene cracker was built and accepted, covering start-up, shutdown and upsets.

tools.name: DYNSIM
tools.role: dynamic process model acting as the virtual plant

build_steps.step: Verify the design heat and material balance, fix the scope to training needs and treat utilities as boundaries.
Mark up P&IDs with system experts, choose which isolation and safety valves to include, then build and join the flowsheets using equipment data.
Run a model acceptance test of the flowsheets against the marked-up P&IDs, without complex control loops, logging a punch list.
Import DCS graphics, controls and shutdown logic from the plant into the simulator.
At factory acceptance, trigger each malfunction from steady state and compare with expected response; repeat testing on site.
Have experienced panel operators shut the model down and start it up again through the DCS graphics.

key_choices.value: Soave-Redlich-Kwong.
Performance curves for rotating machines, actual exchanger and column geometry, and vessel heat loss so that shutdown cooling is represented.

profiles.tool_chain: Design heat and material balance and P&IDs build the DYNSIM model; plant data are used to realign it; DCS and ESD logic are linked through vendor software into the training stations.

validation.detail: Steady-state plant values compared with design balance and two model versions; initial mismatches came from set points and balance data that differed from the operating plant and were corrected using plant data. No quantitative transient agreement reported.

limitations.text: A model built from design mass and energy balances did not reflect the operating plant and had to be realigned to plant data.
Testing quality suffers when testers do not know the plant and its control system; experienced panel operators are needed.

profiles.lesson: For a simulator of an existing plant, calibrate to operating data and actual controller set points from the start, and budget experienced operators for acceptance testing of start-up and shutdown.
profiles.caveats: Short paper with little numerical detail; the closing claim of accurate transient behaviour is not backed by transient data in the text; software version not stated.

profiles.title: Modellierung des Abbrandverhaltens von Ein- und Mehrkomponentenbrennstoffen unter Verbrennungsbedingungen in Poolfeuern
profiles.read_scope: German text: section 6.1 (results and liquid-grid sensitivity), chapter 7 (FireFOAM coupling and results) and chapter 8; earlier theory and experiment chapters not read
profiles.objective: Model the transient evaporation rate of single and multi-component pool fires and couple it to FireFOAM so that the CFD flame heat feedback drives the fuel inlet.

tools.name: FireFOAM (OpenFOAM)
tools.role: LES of an n-heptane pool fire, supplying heat feedback to the evaporation model

tools.name: MATLAB
tools.role: Liquid-phase evaporation model returning burning rate and surface temperature

tools.name: ICEM-CFD
tools.role: Mesh generation

build_steps.step: Define the pool surface as an externally coupled inlet for fuel velocity and temperature.
Start the CFD from a small initial burning rate and exchange data every second of simulated time, computing evaporation from the CFD convective and radiative heat flux.
Build a block domain scaled on pool diameter D (11 D wide, 20 D high) with a circular fuel inlet.
Compare the coupled burning rate with both the uncoupled evaporation model and the measurement to isolate the source of error.

key_choices.value: LES, as implemented in FireFOAM.
Eddy dissipation model with infinitely fast chemistry and a single global heptane reaction.
Finite-volume discrete ordinates with the gas treated as grey.
260 000 hexahedral cells.
Adaptive, with maximum Courant number 1.

profiles.tool_chain: Two-way loop: FireFOAM surface heat flux goes to the MATLAB evaporation model, which returns fuel inlet velocity and surface temperature to FireFOAM.

validation.detail: The stand-alone evaporation model differed from measured boiling-phase burning rates by 8% (n-heptane) and 2% (ethanol), with larger deviations in start-up and preheating. The coupled FireFOAM run gave a burning rate almost twice both the uncoupled calculation and experiment; its surface heat input was about twice that of the uncoupled calculation, and the author attributes this to over-predicted radiative and convective heat input.

sensitivity.detail: For the stand-alone evaporation model: liquid-phase cell count (20 to 200; 50 chosen), initial temperature, pool geometry, mass-transfer coefficient and Lewis number, Stefan flow and ignition energy. No gas-phase CFD mesh study was seen in the sections read.

limitations.text: Small errors in flame heat input strongly change the computed burning rate, and the coupled FireFOAM heat input was too high.
The author suggests more detailed combustion and radiation models could improve agreement.

profiles.lesson: Do not assume a coupled, predictive burning rate is better than a prescribed one: check the surface heat feedback on its own first, because evaporation amplifies its error.
profiles.caveats: Useful as a reported failure. Small laboratory pool only. No gas-phase grid study was found in the parts read, so mesh error cannot be separated from model error.

profiles.title: Benchmark Analysis of Accident Modelling Software Applied to Hydrogen Storage
profiles.read_scope: abstract, chapter 5 (method), jet dispersion study, large-scale jet fire modelling set-up, parts of the jet fire results, and chapter 7
profiles.objective: Benchmark three consequence tools against published hydrogen jet dispersion and jet fire experiments.

tools.name: Phast
tools.role: Hydrogen jet dispersion and jet fire

tools.name: HyRAM+
tools.role: Hydrogen plume dispersion and jet flame length and radiation

tools.name: ALOHA
tools.role: Large jet fire runs (radiation contours and flame length) and a direct-source flammable-contour run using Phast discharge rates; could not produce results for most small and medium jets

build_steps.step: Choose experiments as ground truth for completeness of set-up data and ease of extracting results.
State an assumption for every missing input, such as tank volume, gas temperature and stability class.
Where weather and release height are unknown, vary them in the tool that accepts them and see which dominates.
Pass the discharge coefficient computed by one tool into the tool that requires it as input.
Transform sensor coordinates into each tool's axis system before comparing radiation.
Compare predictions with measured values on scatter plots.

key_choices.item: Assumed storage for the small-jet tests
key_choices.value: A pressurised tank equivalent to 50 L, because the paper did not give the volume.
Class F (moderately stable) for the night-time tests.
Class D, judged from an overcast site photograph.
ALOHA run at 1 m/s because the measured 0.83 m/s was below its limit.
Source term from a vessel run, then a standalone jet fire model for radiation at sensor positions.

profiles.tool_chain: Phast discharge results give the discharge coefficient for HyRAM, tank settings and flow data for ALOHA trials, and the source term for a standalone Phast jet fire calculation.

validation.detail: Both Phast and HyRAM generally underestimated centreline hydrogen concentration, Phast less so, with discrepancy growing at higher concentration. Both generally overpredicted flame length. HyRAM radiation was consistently low; for Phast the abstract and conclusions describe its radiation errors differently. For the large jet fires, ALOHA flame lengths (2 and 5 m) were far below the measured 17.4 and 48.5 m, which the author attributes to its jet fire model being designed for upward vertical releases.

sensitivity.detail: Wind speed had more effect than release height on Phast concentrations at the heights and speeds tried. For the flame-length cases, changing atmospheric stability class affected Phast dispersion but not its jet fire results.

limitations.text: Assumed atmospheric and wind inputs add uncertainty.
Concentrations were read from published log-scale graphs, which may add error.
ALOHA could not handle most of the small and medium jet experiments.

profiles.lesson: Keep a table of assumed inputs next to each benchmark case and do not assume a screening tool covers the case; a non-conservative concentration bias matters when distances to flammable limits are the output.
profiles.caveats: Student thesis with many assumed inputs and graph-digitised data; no statistical measures seen in the parts read. The abstract says Phast overpredicted large jet fire radiation, whereas the conclusions say it overpredicted in one test and underpredicted in another.

profiles.title: Atmospheric Dispersion Model Validation in Low Wind Conditions
