profiles.read_scope: abstract, chapter 1, parts of chapter 2, chapters 3-5
profiles.objective: Test ALOHA, EPIcode and SCIPUFF against near-field releases of three gases in winds mostly below 2 m/s.

tools.name: ALOHA
tools.role: One of three models under test.

tools.name: EPIcode
tools.role: Comparison model.

tools.name: SCIPUFF
tools.role: Comparison model.

build_steps.step: Release each gas as repeated short and long releases, to represent puffs and plumes, inside rings of point sensors.
Use time-averaged release rate and wind from a wind-sensor array as model inputs.
Assign stability class from the measured standard deviation of wind direction.
Compare the highest two-minute average on each ring with predicted centreline concentration.
Score with FAC2, correlation, NMSE, fractional bias, VG and MG, split by distance, flow rate, species and release duration.

key_choices.value: 0.0003 m for the dry lake bed, from published guidance.

profiles.tool_chain: Same measured inputs were given to the three models separately.

validation.detail: Factor-of-two fractions over all data were 0.4000 for ALOHA, 0.4583 for EPIcode and 0.4250 for SCIPUFF, with low correlation coefficients; the author finds ALOHA biased to under-prediction.

sensitivity.detail: Results are stratified by distance, flow rate, species and duration; model inputs were not varied.

limitations.text: ALOHA forced a higher wind speed than observed in 19 of 30 experiments because of its minimum for the stability class, which the author gives as a reason for its under-prediction.
ALOHA is not designed for these low-wind conditions and tended to under-predict, so it needs caution.
Some detector points rose with distance because of meander, lofting and sensor spacing; denser arrays are needed.

profiles.lesson: Log the inputs the tool actually used, not only those you wanted to enter: a forced higher wind speed changes the comparison and, per the author, lowered ALOHA's predicted concentrations.
profiles.caveats: The species discussion describes the SCIPUFF geometric-mean-bias values as under-prediction, while Table 8 lists values below 1, which the report defines as over-prediction. Table 6B prints the same 100 m MG (1.4227) for ALOHA and EPIcode. The report uses ammonia as its buoyant-gas case. Small releases (mean rates under about 20 kg/h) and ranges to 100 m only.

tools.role: Estimated the expanded jet area used to size the leak-region cells

Represent all objects, including small ones, in the geometry before gridding.
Estimate the expanded jet area first, then size the leak cell so the jet sits in one cell no more than twice its area.
Grade from fine leak cells to the coarse macro grid, limiting the cell-to-cell change.
Place monitor points at the field sensor positions and compare with a factor-of-two criterion and time traces.

Extends 50 m along the jet, starting just upstream of the release.

key_choices.item: Recommended macro cell size for similar dense-gas cases

Held constant, although measured speed and direction varied widely during the trials.
Guideline value 20 for dispersion; may be raised with local refinement but lowered again if unstable.

profiles.tool_chain: A one-dimensional jet utility sizes the leak cells; the time-dependent release rate from the trial drives FLACS; monitor outputs are compared with oxygen-sensor-derived concentrations.

validation.detail: New LPG trials, one open and one with a fence. FAC2 for centreline peaks 75% and 83%, for all working sensors 70% and 72%; the author quotes mean errors of 13% (unobstructed) and 18% (obstructed) at a snapshot. Concentrations 2 m from the release were badly under-predicted.

limitations.text: The simulated cloud diluted faster than measured and missed accumulation linked to wind variation.
The guiding principles apply to dense-gas releases with obstacles similar to those studied.

profiles.lesson: Size the leak cell from the expanded jet, refine the vertical direction for dense gas, and do not expect a steady-wind run to reproduce light, shifting-wind transients.
profiles.caveats: Only two usable trials. The guideline chapter limits micro-cell aspect ratio to below two while the field-test chapter states no larger than five and uses 0.04 m by 0.20 m cells. The 13% and 18% errors describe one instant, not the whole record.

profiles.title: Uncertainty Quantification and Sensitivity Analysis for Quantitative Risk Assessments of Hydrogen Infrastructure
profiles.read_scope: chapter 1 methodology, chapter 2 results (overview and sensitivity conclusions, cases 3-4), chapter 3 summary, appendix A
profiles.objective: Propagate input uncertainty through the HyRAM+ default hydrogen QRA and rank which inputs drive potential loss of life.

tools.name: HyRAM+
tools.role: Deterministic QRA engine evaluated repeatedly with sampled inputs.

tools.name: SciPy Latin hypercube sampler
tools.role: Generated the input samples.

build_steps.step: Define the system as a component count (valves, instruments, joints, hose, pipe lengths) with state conditions and fuelling demand.
Combine component leak frequencies per leak size with fault trees, then use an event sequence diagram to reach jet fire, explosion, no ignition or shutdown.
Give leak frequencies, dispenser failure probabilities and occupant positions distributions, and sample them with Latin hypercube sampling.
Compare the sampled risk distribution with the deterministic result.
Separate occupant location as an outer epistemic loop so that other sensitivities can be ranked by linear regression, checked with scatter plots.

key_choices.value: Five sizes from 0.01 to 100 percent of pipe flow area.
Flow-rate bands with immediate values 0.008, 0.053 and 0.23 and delayed values 0.004, 0.027 and 0.12.
BST method with Mach flame speed 0.35 for delayed ignition.
Eisenberg thermal probit with a 30 s exposure (an overpressure head-impact probit is also used).
Probability 0.9 that a release is detected and mitigated before posing risk.
Nine, uniformly distributed 1-20 m along and 1-12 m across the jet axis.

profiles.tool_chain: Sampled inputs go through repeated HyRAM+ QRA runs, then regression and scatter-plot analysis.

validation.detail: No comparison with data or another code. Only a consistency check: the deterministic result was verified with both the HyRAM+ Python backend and the GUI.

sensitivity.detail: Occupant location dominates; once conditioned on location, full-bore leak frequencies of instruments and then joints lead. Doubling pressure had little effect on the rankings.

limitations.text: Only parametric uncertainty in selected inputs was treated; physical release model and implicit assumption uncertainties were not.
Linear regression in single-loop sampling probably understates the effect of strongly nonlinear location variables.
Published hydrogen failure frequency data are scarce.

profiles.lesson: Report a hydrogen QRA result with a percentile band, and treat where people stand as part of the scenario definition. A two-loop design stops location from hiding frequency sensitivities.
profiles.caveats: The report gives different low ends for the risk spread in two places (to about 1e-14 in the results, about 1e-12 in the summary). Demonstration case is the tool default system, not a real site.

profiles.title: Validation of the HyRAM+ physics models for use with propane
profiles.read_scope: abstract, introduction, chapter 2 model description, start of flame length, heat flux section, trajectory text, conclusions
profiles.objective: Check HyRAM+ jet flame length, heat flux, flame trajectory and unignited dispersion against published propane experiments.

tools.name: HyRAM+
tools.version: not stated (cites the version 3.0 technical reference manual)
tools.role: Model under validation, driven through Python objects.

tools.name: CoolProp
tools.role: Propane thermodynamic properties for the leak calculation.

build_steps.step: Take experiment conditions from each paper as inputs and fill gaps with stated assumptions or calculations.
Where pressure and mass flow disagree, keep the measured mass flow and back-calculate pressure.
Compare flame lengths and widths across several independent datasets.
Compute heat flux twice, with predicted and with measured flame length, to expose compensating errors.
Compare centreline concentration, velocity and radial profiles for unignited jets.

key_choices.value: Isentropic orifice flow with the default Yuceil-Otugen notional nozzle only.
CoolProp near the leak, ideal gas elsewhere.

profiles.tool_chain: Orifice flow feeds the notional nozzle, then the jet or flame model.

validation.detail: Conclusions: flame lengths and widths over-predicted by around 65% in three of four cases, the fourth closer to 20% off. Heat flux was closer with the over-long predicted flame (errors around 65%) than with the measured length (closer to 85%). Flame trajectory matched at the high Reynolds number but buoyancy was much over-predicted at the lower one. Unignited centreline mole fraction was within 15%, with radial profiles wider than measured.

sensitivity.detail: No sensitivity study beyond the two flame-length variants for heat flux.

limitations.text: The data are low-pressure; more validation is needed at propane autogas storage pressures.
All dispersion cases were unchoked, so choked flows remain unvalidated.
Flame length and heat flux errors offset, so correcting one requires correcting the other.

profiles.lesson: Validate intermediate quantities (flame length) as well as the end quantity (heat flux); otherwise compensating errors pass unnoticed.
profiles.caveats: The percentage statements are not equivalent: sections 3 and 5 say measured flame lengths were about 65% of the predicted lengths, while the abstract and conclusions speak of over-prediction by around 65%. Section 3 describes five flame-length sources (one within about 20%, four with measured about 65% of predicted); the conclusions say three of four cases were over-predicted by about 65% and the fourth was closer to 20% off. The dispersion cases were all unchoked and the flame data were at low source pressure.

profiles.title: Risk assessment of a liquid storage terminal: comparison of Brazilian and Dutch methodologies
profiles.read_scope: whole paper
profiles.objective: Re-run a published Dutch benchmark flammable-liquid depot under both Brazilian CETESB P4.261 rules and Dutch rules, and explain the differences in risk.

tools.name: Safeti
tools.role: Updated Dutch-method risk calculation and Brazilian-method risk.

tools.name: Phast
tools.role: Consequence distances under the Brazilian method.

build_steps.step: Reuse a published fictitious depot with its layout, surrounding population and ignition sources.
Change only the aspects and criteria specific to the second country, keeping the rest of the base case.
Assign representative substances by the national rules, and screen out low-hazard liquids from the QRA.
First re-run the home method in the newer software version to isolate the version effect.
Trace contour differences back to individual effect distances for the dominant tank scenarios.

key_choices.value: BEVI manual for equipment and CONCAWE data for pipelines.
n-decane for crude oil, n-hexane for gasoline, n-nonane for jet fuel.
TNO multi-energy with unconfined strength 10 and 10 percent efficiency.
Thermal exposure capped at 20 s for pool and jet fires in the probit.

profiles.tool_chain: Phast/Safeti consequence results feed Safeti individual and societal risk.

validation.detail: Dutch-method hazard distances were compared between Safeti 6.54 (published) and 9.0, with no consistent direction of change.

sensitivity.detail: No formal sensitivity study; differences are attributed to substance choice, ignition probability and software version.

profiles.lesson: Record the software version with every risk contour and re-baseline after upgrades. In this comparison the authors link the main Brazil-Netherlands differences to the representative substance for crude oil and the immediate-ignition probability.
profiles.caveats: Short conference paper. Weather frequencies and risk grid settings were not found in the text (the hazard table uses D5 and F1.5). The paper says the version 9.0 Dutch-method and CETESB hazard distances were very similar except for Tank 01, but tabulates distances for Tank 01 only. The authors say a more detailed analysis of one difference in the pump and loading areas was not feasible because some radiation ranges were not reported in the original work. The 1e-6 per year contour around the crude tank is reported at about 250 m with version 9.0 against about 160 m with 6.54, and the originally published F-N curve shows more fatalities. The text read is a reading-order re-extraction of the saved PDF.

profiles.title: Blind-prediction: estimating the consequences of vented hydrogen deflagrations for homogeneous mixtures in 20-foot ISO containers
profiles.institution_or_venue: 7th International Conference on Hydrogen Safety (ICHS2017), Hamburg
profiles.read_scope: whole paper (figures read only through the text, apart from the discussion page, which was viewed as an image to check a number)
profiles.objective: Compare blind predictions from CFD tools and a phenomenological model, submitted before the experiments were complete, with vented hydrogen deflagration tests in shipping containers; engineering-correlation results, not part of the original blind study, are also compared.

tools.name: FLACS
tools.role: CFD predictions by several modellers

tools.name: ANSYS CFX
tools.role: CFD predictions

tools.name: IMPETUS Afea Solver
tools.role: Structural response of container walls, loaded from FLACS results

tools.name: Engineering correlations (NFPA 68, EN 14994, FM Global, Molkov forms)
tools.version: as referenced in the paper's Table 3
tools.role: Simple venting predictions

build_steps.step: Define simple, fully specified explosion scenarios and collect predictions with a deadline before the experiments are completed.
Repeat each experimental scenario so that experimental scatter can be shown next to model scatter.
Record each submission's code version, grid and special settings.
For structural response, pass CFD pressure-time loads one way to a structural solver or to a simple static estimate.
Compare pressure histories and sensor scatter with bands of plus or minus 30% and a factor of two, and compare maxima against the experimental spread.

key_choices.value: Quiescent homogeneous 15 vol.% hydrogen in air, back-wall ignition, doors open, with and without a bottle basket obstacle.
Chosen by each modeller; one automatically generated grid did not follow the tool's guidance for confined explosions and should have been twice as fine.
Treating the bottle basket as one obstacle followed the experimental trend better than other treatments.

profiles.tool_chain: CFD pressure loads from one submission feed a structural finite element solver, and from another a static deflection formula; all predictions are collected centrally and compared with measurements.

validation.detail: The authors say most predictions from the CFD tools and phenomenological model agreed reasonably with experiment and all captured the obstacle's pressure increase, but highest and lowest predictions differed by a ratio of about 23 in both scenarios. Engineering models, which were not part of the blind study, had ratios below 10 and did better overall for these simple scenarios.

sensitivity.detail: Several modellers submitted multiple grids; the same CFD tool showed large scatter across users and grid resolutions.

limitations.text: Pressure measurements had noise and drift and several were discarded.
Using one container for all six tests affects repeatability, especially of structural measurements.
The better showing of engineering models may not carry over to more complex cases.
It could not be determined whether other CFD codes show the same user spread, since each had one modeller group.

profiles.lesson: Do not treat one CFD run as the answer for vented explosion pressure: follow the tool's grid rules, show results for more than one resolution or analyst, and compare with a simple correlation.
profiles.caveats: Lean, low-pressure tests (relatively weak explosions) with weak signals. Coordinated by the vendor of one of the tools. One withdrawn and one resubmitted non-blind prediction. Covers only the first of two blind studies.

profiles.title: SMEDIS Final Report (draft): Scientific Model Evaluation of Dense Gas Dispersion Models
authors: SMEDIS project partners (coordinated by HSE, with CERC and EdF as main partners)
profiles.institution_or_venue: EU SMEDIS project; draft hosted by the Atmospheric Dispersion Modelling Liaison Committee
profiles.read_scope: chapter 1, the conclusions of chapter 2, most of chapter 4 (database, validation procedure, results, conclusion) and part of the data selection appendix
profiles.objective: Develop and test a protocol for independent evaluation of dense gas dispersion models (scientific assessment, verification, validation), with emphasis on aerosols, obstacles and complex terrain.

tools.name: Dense gas dispersion models in four classes (screening, integral, shallow-layer, CFD)
tools.version: versions listed per model in the report's Table 1.1
tools.role: Subjects of evaluation: 28 models

tools.name: REDIPHEM database
tools.role: Main source of processed experimental data

build_steps.step: Write a Model Evaluation Report for each model from a uniform template, using only developer-supplied information and agreeing it with the developer.
Select validation datasets by questionnaire to partners on prior use, availability and quality.
Classify candidate scenarios by source type, complex effect, gas density and atmosphere, and pick cases to cover the cells.
Fix the cases each model class must run, with fewer for shallow-layer and CFD models than for integral and screening tools.
Compare both arc-wise and point-wise quantities, using paired measures of bias and scatter plus factor-of-n fractions.
Require users to document setup, changed parameters and any model modifications, and to use one model version for all runs.

key_choices.value: Mean relative bias and mean relative square error as principal measures, supported by factor-of-n fractions; geometric measures kept for comparison with earlier work.
Users were given the observations, because model improvement during the project was allowed.
Users could voluntarily run cases their model could not properly represent, to see the effect, with such mismatches flagged.
Allowed alongside field trials, with tunnel cases scaled to full-size equivalents.

profiles.tool_chain: Developer information feeds the assessment report; processed datasets are issued as spreadsheet workbooks; model proponents return results in a template; two partners compute statistics centrally and add them to each evaluation report.

validation.detail: Preliminary analysis of the first set of results. Point-wise scores were lower than arc-wise scores. The authors conclude that FAC2 and the spread measures generally improved with model complexity; the chapter body notes that shallow-layer models were an exception for spread, and that on the bias measures integral models looked best except for terrain. Some groups had small samples.

sensitivity.detail: None in the parts read.

limitations.text: Only the first result set was fully analysed, for lack of resources.
There are large gaps in data for dense gas releases with complex effects, especially without wind-tunnel data.
Assessments used only supplied documents, often poorly organised, and the models themselves were not run by assessors.
Measurement uncertainty, needed to define acceptable agreement, was not always available.

profiles.lesson: Report arc-wise and point-wise scores separately, state whether predictions were blind, and flag every run outside a model's stated applicability; each of these changes what a pass score means.
profiles.caveats: A draft with placeholders, typographic errors and model identities removed from results; do not cite its numbers as final. Validation was not blind and many proponents were developers. The year is taken from file path markers and workshop date in the text.

profiles.title: On numerical modelling of atmospheric gas dispersion using CFD approach
profiles.institution_or_venue: Nanyang Technological University, School of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering
profiles.read_scope: abstract, start of chapter 4 (flat-terrain boundary layer set-up), chapter 5 and chapter 6
profiles.objective: Build an OpenFOAM atmospheric boundary layer and dense gas dispersion model and evaluate it for LNG vapour against wind-tunnel and field data.

tools.name: OpenFOAM
tools.role: Custom boundary layer and gas dispersion solvers

tools.name: CoolProp
tools.role: Temperature-dependent properties of air and methane

tools.name: FLACS (published results)
tools.role: Code-to-code comparator through statistics taken from the literature

build_steps.step: First show that the inlet wind and turbulence profiles stay the same along an empty domain, using mesh, turbulence-model and roughness studies.
Run a steady boundary layer solution before the transient gas release and use it as the initial field.
Do mesh studies on peak concentration separately for the wind-tunnel and field cases.
Derive the LNG spill source from an assumed vaporisation rate with reported spill mass and duration, giving pool diameter and vapour flow.
Tune ground heat transfer and turbulent Schmidt number on one field test, then apply the chosen set to the other tests.
Score with the LNG protocol's statistical measures and compare with published commercial-code scores.

key_choices.value: RANS, with modified k-epsilon performing better than SST k-omega for unobstructed cases.
Calibrated: 0.3 for wind-tunnel dense gas and 0.15 for LNG, much below the solver default of 1.
Assumed 0.167 kg per square metre per second for the Burro spill source.
Fixed temperature, giving most heat input, chosen as it best matched peaks and offsets neglected latent and radiative heat.

profiles.tool_chain: A steady boundary layer solver gives initial and inlet fields to the transient dispersion solver; a hand source calculation sets the vapour inlet; CoolProp supplies property fits; scores are compared with published FLACS values.

validation.detail: Hamburg wind-tunnel and Burro field tests. The author reports all protocol statistical measures within acceptance ranges and better scores than published FLACS values. The conclusions call near-source peaks quite conservative, whereas chapter 5 also reports under-prediction at 57 m for Burro8 and describes the Burro9 arc-wise result as under-predicted (accurate at 800 m). Parameters were tuned on DA0120 and Burro9, which are among the scored tests.

sensitivity.detail: Mesh, turbulence model, roughness, ground heat model and turbulent Schmidt number; the Schmidt number had a significant effect, and the coarsest Burro mesh agreed better than finer ones before retuning.

limitations.text: Validation covers only unobstructed tests.
Only neutral stratification is validated for the boundary layer model.
The LNG source is single phase, not a two-phase spill.
The assumed source term may account for much of the near-source error.

profiles.lesson: Keep calibration and validation cases separate. Parameters tuned on a test, including one that compensates missing physics, make that test's pass scores weaker evidence.
profiles.caveats: Key parameters were selected on DA0120 and Burro9, which are also among the scored tests. Tuned Schmidt numbers differ between the wind-tunnel and LNG cases. FLACS scores are taken from the literature; for the wind-tunnel comparison the author notes that FLACS was validated on larger tests, so the sets may not match. The tables label the scatter measure RMSE although the acceptance range matches the protocol's mean relative square error.

profiles.title: Modelling of a low emission thermally integrated gasifier for clean gas production from agricultural and forestry residues
profiles.read_scope: abstract and chapter 4 (model description, validation, start of results) and its conclusions
profiles.objective: Model a two-stage thermally integrated steam gasifier for hardwood in UniSim and check whether heat from the hot stage can drive the low-temperature stage.

tools.name: UniSim Design
tools.role: Steady-state two-stage gasification model.

build_steps.step: Define biomass as a hypothetical solid from literature proximate and ultimate analyses.
Split the process into a low-temperature and a high-temperature stage with separate reactor modules.
Specify oxidation-type steps as conversion reactions and methanation, shift and reforming as equilibrium reactions.
Validate only the low-temperature stage against laboratory char yields, averaging scattered replicates.
Represent heat conduction through a dividing wall with a pair of linked exchangers, since the tool cannot transfer heat directly between units.

key_choices.value: Peng-Robinson, justified by earlier gasification studies.
Adiabatic gasification stages.
20% assumed in transfer from stage 2 to stage 1.

validation.detail: Low-temperature stage only, against the author's heating-chamber experiments at 10, 15 and 20 l/min air: carbon error 1.6% to 6.4%; gas production error up to 10.62%. The integrated concept and high-temperature stage are not validated.

sensitivity.detail: Air flow, high-temperature stage temperature and steam/biomass ratio (1.0 to 4.0) varied for heat transfer, syngas composition and heating value.

limitations.text: The tool cannot represent biomass physical structure, dust or impurities.
Tar cannot be analysed with this model.
The author says an equilibrium model suffices for the proof-of-concept scope, but detailed kinetic, particle and reactor models are required.

profiles.lesson: Say which part of a flowsheet the data actually test; agreement on one stage's solid yield says little about downstream gas composition.
profiles.caveats: The abstract has an unfinished validation sentence (dots in place of text). At 10 l/min the section 4.5 text gives 123 g of carbon from experiment and 125 g from the model, while Table 20 lists 125 g experimental and 123 g UniSim. The text gives a maximum gas-production error of 10.7% and Table 22 lists 10.62%. The assumption list gives a biomass flow of 1 kg/h, while Table 19 lists 10 kg/h. UniSim version not stated.

profiles.title: Evaluation of IPS guidelines regarding Quantitative Risk Analysis

profiles.objective: Test the Swedish IPS QRA guideline by applying it to a fictitious ammonia plant and judging how usable it is.

tools.name: RiskCurves (spelt RiskCurve in the thesis)

build_steps.step: Take generic loss-of-containment scenarios by equipment type from the BEVI manual, and add specific ones from a HAZID.
Screen pipelines, keeping only long ones or those crossing a road.
Enter weather as a combined matrix of wind direction, wind speed and stability class.
Build population as separate residential and operating areas with day and night fractions and time present.
Check that the models and vulnerability criteria selected in the software match what the guideline prescribes.
Run one-at-a-time sensitivity on influential inputs, then test relocation and smaller storage tanks as risk reductions.

key_choices.value: BEVI for most components, with site data preferred when it exists.
Set to 1e-3 as a conservative judgement because it could not be derived.
BEVI delayed-ignition method is recommended only with SAFETI; IOGP is the second, for petroleum-based products; the Moosemiller method is given for other substances.
Calculated instead of taking standard values, because toxicity dominated the pure-ammonia results.
Guideline pairs of wind speed and day/night stability, for example 2 m/s with B by day and F by night, 5 m/s with C or D; wind rose supplied for the site.
Guideline recommends 50 x 50 m cells.

key_choices.item: risk criteria for a new site
key_choices.value: Individual risk upper limit 1e-6 per year and negligible level 1e-8 per year.

profiles.tool_chain: Single tool: RiskCurves.

validation.detail: No validation; the inputs and settings were checked by a supervisor.

sensitivity.detail: Filling degree, surface roughness, population data and pump/compressor failure frequency varied one at a time. Population changes left individual risk unchanged (expected); roughness and filling degree visibly changed the contours. None breached the upper societal limit; population and roughness are judged most influential.

limitations.text: The software behaves largely as a black box; the equations used for source strength could not be traced against the guideline.
Equipment density, which drives delayed ignition probability, is a subjective choice.
The author is employed by a consultancy that helped develop the guideline, and the tool vendor supplied the licence.

profiles.lesson: Treat surface roughness as a first-class uncertainty in toxic-dominated risk contours. Report which ignition-probability method was used and whether it is tied to a particular software.
profiles.caveats: Master's thesis on a fictitious site. The method states a factor-of-two variation; Table 3.2 lists filling degree as 40, 80 and 100% under the halved, original and doubled columns. The results call pumps prominent contributors to the risk and also report that changing pump and compressor frequency did not result in larger individual risk. No numerical contour distances to reproduce were found in the saved text.

profiles.title: Validation of PHAST Dispersion Model as Required for USA LNG Siting Applications
profiles.read_scope: whole paper
profiles.objective: Summarise the validation of the Phast Unified Dispersion Model against the LNG model evaluation protocol database for US siting approval.

tools.name: Phast (UDM dispersion with PVAP pool model)
tools.role: Model under validation.

build_steps.step: Take the experiment list from the prescribed evaluation protocol and state for each how it is represented in the model.
Represent LNG field spills as low-momentum elevated horizontal releases with almost complete immediate rainout, so a pool forms.
Split time-varying pool evaporation into constant-rate segments, and pick the segment to match the averaging window.
Compute MG, VG, relative bias and error, factor-of-two fraction and safety factors on concentration, width and distance to LFL.
Submit input-uncertainty sensitivity (wind, stability, roughness, pressure, humidity, composition) with the statistics.

key_choices.value: Roughness 0.0002 m; pool on shallow water.
Pure methane in the example input table.
Approval recommends using half LFL, consistent with Phast defaults for flammables.

profiles.tool_chain: Discharge/pool rate segments from PVAP feed the UDM dispersion calculation.

validation.detail: Authors report excellent short-average Burro and Coyote results and under-prediction for Maplin Sands; for long averages, excellent Thorney Island, good Burro and over-predicted Coyote concentrations; wind-tunnel concentrations consistently under-predicted with slightly over-predicted widths. Cited earlier work on a wider large-scale set (overlapping these field tests) gives overall agreement within a factor of two.

sensitivity.detail: Sensitivity to experimental input uncertainty was part of the submission; results are not given in this paper.

limitations.text: Phast assumes uniform roughness, so approval notes it may be unsuitable for high aspect-ratio pools, highly varying terrain or large obstacles.
Long averaging times with strongly time-varying pools are hard to model with the segment approach.

profiles.lesson: State the segment-selection and averaging-time rule alongside any validation score, because the score depends on it. Check wind-tunnel and field results separately.
profiles.caveats: Vendor-authored summary. The conclusions describe over-prediction for the scaled wind-tunnel experiments, while the results section says concentrations were consistently under-predicted there; the wind-tunnel MG values in Table 4 (defined as observed over predicted) are above 1, in line with the results section. The suggested explanation for the Maplin Sands and wind-tunnel results relies partly on verbal communication with the regulators.

profiles.title: Modeling and Control of Post-Combustion CO2 Capture Process Integrated with a 550MWe Supercritical Coal-fired Power Plant
profiles.read_scope: abstract, literature review (parts), chapters 3 and 4 (to the pressure-drop model), conclusions and future work; control chapters 5-7 only through the conclusions
profiles.objective: Build steady-state (Aspen Plus) and pressure-driven dynamic (Aspen Plus Dynamics) models of MEA capture integrated with a supercritical coal plant, then design PID, linear and nonlinear MPC and robust controllers.

tools.name: Aspen Plus (RateSep)
tools.role: Rate-based steady-state capture model used for sizing and optimisation.

tools.name: Aspen Plus Dynamics
tools.role: Equilibrium-based pressure-driven dynamic model and control test bed.

tools.name: Aspen Exchanger Design & Rating
tools.role: Sized exchangers to give hold-up volumes and metal mass.

build_steps.step: Build and optimise the rate-based steady-state model by sensitivity runs on temperatures, lean loading, pressures and packing height.
Before export, size columns, exchangers and vessels and add volumes and metal mass, because they set accumulation rates.
Connect units through flow devices so that pressure and flow can be solved together.
Replace rate-based columns by equilibrium columns and correct them with a fitted CO2 Murphree efficiency correlation checked against the rate-based model off design.
Replace the default dynamic packing pressure-drop equation with a fitted correlation so off-design hydraulics match the steady-state model.
Identify reduced models from the dynamic simulation for use inside model-predictive control.

key_choices.value: Electrolyte NRTL for the liquid and Redlich-Kwong for the vapour in the rate-based model.
CO2 absorption and desorption reactions kinetically controlled, the rest at equilibrium in steady state.
Kinetic reactions replaced by equilibrium reactions with literature equilibrium constants, as the dynamic tool does not support the rate-based tower.
Two trains only, although three to six are needed, because of computing cost.
Random packing in the absorber and structured in the stripper, because the Aspen Plus model was considered validated for that arrangement.

profiles.tool_chain: Rate-based Aspen Plus results size the plant and calibrate efficiency and pressure-drop correlations; the exported Aspen Plus Dynamics model is then used to identify linear and nonlinear models for controllers.

validation.detail: The equilibrium dynamic model with fitted efficiency and pressure-drop corrections is compared with the rate-based model (parity plots, good match). The abstract also says the steady-state model is validated with pilot-plant data, but no such comparison was found in the sections read or by text search.

sensitivity.detail: Steady-state sensitivity on temperatures, loading, stripper and absorber pressure and packing height, used to lower reboiler heat duty from 4.05 to 3.07 GJ/ton CO2.

limitations.text: The dynamic tool lacks the rate-based column model, forcing the equilibrium substitute and corrections.
The default steam turbine performance curve is only an approximation for load-following dynamics.
MEA degradation is not modelled.

profiles.lesson: When moving from rate-based steady state to an equilibrium dynamic model, test the two against each other over the whole disturbance range, including hydraulics, not only at the design point.
profiles.caveats: The abstract says the steady-state model is validated with pilot-plant data; no such comparison was found in the sections read or by a text search of the saved text. No comparison of the dynamic results with plant or experimental data was found. Software versions not stated.

profiles.title: Modeling of depressurization-induced superheating for compressed liquefied gases
profiles.institution_or_venue: Industrial & Engineering Chemistry Research (accepted manuscript, UCL Discovery)
profiles.read_scope: introduction, model theory, numerical method, validation, parameter studies, conclusions
profiles.objective: Develop a two-zone blowdown model that allows the liquid to stay superheated during rapid depressurisation of CO2 and CO2 mixtures.

tools.name: REFPROP (GERG-2004 EoS)
tools.role: thermodynamic and transport properties

tools.name: BLOWSIM
tools.role: comparison blowdown code without liquid superheat

build_steps.step: Write separate mole and entropy-based energy balances for vapour and liquid zones, with condensate dropping instantly into the liquid.
Delay liquid flashing with a linear relaxation law toward equilibrium vapour fraction, governed by a relaxation time.
Select the choked discharge sub-model by the phase at the orifice (vapour, two-phase mass-flux maximisation, or Bernoulli for liquid).
Integrate the ODE system without interphase source terms, then add them explicitly within the same step.
Check time-step convergence and compare pressure and both zone temperatures against two independent experiment sets.

key_choices.value: GERG-2004 rather than cubic equations, for better accuracy near the critical and supercritical region.
Constant, picked in all cases to give the best agreement with the measurements.
Churchill-Chu natural convection to vapour and Rohsenow boiling to liquid; through-wall gradient neglected for steel.
0.001 s time step; relaxation time 0.5 s for the vessel release tests and 0.01 s for the short-pipe tests.

profiles.tool_chain: REFPROP properties feed the two-zone ODE model; results are compared with measurements and with BLOWSIM.

validation.detail: Two experiment sets (vessel releases and short-pipe releases). Authors report good agreement for pressure and both zone temperatures; the relaxation time was fitted to these data and the comparison code under-predicted depressurisation rate.

sensitivity.detail: Relaxation time varied from 0.005 to 0.5 s; orifice diameter and nitrogen impurity varied. Longer relaxation gave more liquid superheat; vapour temperature was not noticeably affected.

limitations.text: No bulk fluid motion is assumed, so pipeline use is limited to isolated lines.
A constant relaxation time is used because data and correlations are lacking; dedicated CO2 correlations are left for future work.
Fire exposure is possible in principle but run time would be prohibitive.

profiles.lesson: If a non-equilibrium blowdown model has a relaxation time chosen to fit the test, treat the agreement as calibration and hold out tests before predicting new geometries or compositions.
profiles.caveats: Accepted manuscript; fitted parameter differs by a factor of 50 between the two test sets; agreement described qualitatively.

profiles.title: Numerical Modelling of the Rapid Depressurisation and Outflow of High Pressure Containments in the Framework of Carbon Capture and Sequestration
profiles.read_scope: contents, chapter 3 (solid CO2 formation: theory, numerics, validation, conclusions), chapter 7 conclusions and start of future work
profiles.objective: Extend transient flow models for rupture and puncture decompression of CO2 pipelines, including solid CO2 formation, non-equilibrium and stratified two-phase flow.

tools.name: in-house homogeneous equilibrium pipe-flow model (finite volume, HLLC solver)
tools.role: decompression and solid fraction prediction

tools.name: GERG 2008 and extended Peng-Robinson EoS
tools.role: properties above and below the CO2 triple point

build_steps.step: Solve conservation of mass, momentum and energy along the pipe, including wall heat transfer and friction.
Set zero velocity at the closed end and obtain the choked rupture-plane condition from local wave relations with isentropic flow.
Replace the equilibrium sound speed, which goes to zero at the triple point, with a homogeneous frozen mixture value.
Verify the solver on a Riemann problem and an independent isentrope analysis before using experimental data.
Check grid convergence, then simulate a full-bore rupture test and compare intact-end pressure and temperature histories.

key_choices.value: 500 cells and CFL 0.5 for the validation run.
Chen friction-factor correlation; Rohsenow correlation on the assumption that boiling dominates.

key_choices.item: flow model choice in other chapters
key_choices.value: Relaxation model for non-equilibrium and a two-fluid model for punctures, each compared with the equilibrium model.

profiles.tool_chain: Equation-of-state flash results feed the finite-volume flow solver; thesis chapter 6 provides jet expansion conditions intended as dispersion model input.

validation.detail: Full-bore rupture pipeline test: temperature agreement good down to the triple point, then degrading, with the model under-predicting CO2 temperature. Pressure agreement is described as excellent; puncture tests in a later chapter are reported as good.

sensitivity.detail: Grid convergence checks and a comparison of two sound-speed formulations.

limitations.text: The equilibrium assumption breaks down once solids can separate and settle, so predicted solid distribution along the pipe may be wrong.
With a pure-CO2 relaxation-time correlation the non-equilibrium model performed less well.

profiles.lesson: In CO2 blowdown, check how the sound speed and equation of state behave at the triple point, and do not read solid accumulation locations from a homogeneous model.
profiles.caveats: Pipeline outflow for consequence assessment rather than process-vessel blowdown; only chapters 3 and 7 were read in detail; chapter 3 validation uses a single test.
